2.3.3.DS.M.2 Process controls

Manufacturing process description for each process step along with corresponding process parameters (CPPs) and in-process controls (IPCs) that are essential for ensuring that a drug substance of the required quality at each step are given in [[Table 1-1 Process description of Sakuramil manufacturing process]]. Information includes also acceptance criteria and associated test methods.

3.2.DS.M Manufacturing (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]

3.2.DS.M.1 Description of Manufacturing process

Manufacturing process description for each process step along with corresponding CPPs, IPCs and their control ranges/acceptance criteria at each step are given below. Description includes also quantities of raw materials used.

Step 1 (CP-4 to CP-5)

CP-4 (175-185 kg), Methyl chloroformate (55-120 L) are combined. Lithium-tert-butoxide (22-85 kg) is added and stirred. To the mixture, tetrahydrofuran (750-920 L) is added and stirred. The layers are settled and separated. The resulting precipitates are filtered, rinsed with tetrahydrofuran and dried at temperatures up to 50°C to yield CP-5. Yield: Approximately 200 kg of Intermediate CP-5. About 91% in theory

Step 2 (CP-5 to CP-6)

CP-5 (195-210 kg), Sodium borohydride (480-2120 kg), Magnesium chloride (22-35 kg) and methanol (105-320 L) are combined. Upon reaction completion, the mixtures is filtered, and to the filtrate hydrochloric acid (54-59 L) is added and stirred. The layers are settled and separated. The organic layer is concentrated by distillation with ethanol for the solvents exchange (final concentration 1000 L). Water (25 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol) is added and the mixture is stirred at 14 to 26°C. The resulting crystalline precipitates are filtered, rinsed with ethanol, and dried at temperatures up to 50°C to yield CP-6. Yield: About 235 kg of Intermediate CP-6, About 87% in theory

Step 4 (CP-7 and CP-8 to final drug substance)

CP-7 (240-260 kg) and CP-8 (200-220 kg)) are combined in methylene chloride (720-760 L). Tetra-n-butylammonium bromide (49-52 kg) and aqueous sodium hydroxide solution (720-760 L) are added while maintaining the mixture at temperatures between 12 and 25°C. Upon reaction completion, methylene chloride (805-815 L) and water (98-105 L) are added, the mixture is separated, and the organic layer is washed with diluted hydrochloric acid. The organic layer is concentrated and displaced by distillation with ethanol (final concentration 1800L). Water (20 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol) is added to the mixture. This addition of water in the crystallization is considered as CPP #4.1 with an acceptance range of 25 to 35% weight per weight of ethanol. Ethanol content is monitored by IPC #1. After cooling, the mixture is stirred at 14 to 26°C. Cooling rate is considered as CPP #4.2 with an acceptance criteria of 0.15 – 0.5 °C / min and tested in IPC #2. The resulting crystalline precipitates are filtered, rinsed with ethanol, and dried at temperatures up to 50°C to yield CP-9 (Sakuramil). 3.2.DS.M.2 Development of manufacturing process and process control

1 Description of Critical Material Attributes from Starting Materials

1.1 Starting Material 1 - CP-4

CP-4 has been manufactured by IROHA-corp. (China) and HETO-corp. (Germany). CP-4 manufactured at commercial scale has been converted to Sakuramil drug substance that has been used in Phase 3 clinical trials and ICH drug substance stability studies. The quality of CP-4 is tightly controlled in accordance with the commercial specification in section [[2.3.3.SM.C Control [CP-4] [Sakuramil] [CP-6]]] .

Justification for section of CP-4 Starting Material is provided in section [[2.3.4.SM.D Description [CP-4][Sakuramil][CP-6]]].

The desired impurity profile of CP-4 is achieved through the use of a reproducible process and a robust crystallization using a combination of ethanol and water as the final solvent mixture.

All process related impurities present in the SM, CP-4, at levels greater than 0.1 % have been identified and appropriate limits and controls have been established based on demonstrated purge data, design space knowledge, and scale and equipment considerations in the subsequent synthetic steps. Individual unspecified impurities are controlled in lots of CP-4 to levels of NMT 0.5 %. CP-4 is not a source of impurities (≥ 0.15%) in the drug substance.

Stability evaluation of CP-4 has demonstrated that CP-4 is stable with no observations of significant degradation. An informal study of the stability of CP-6 under conditions of 30°C/65% RH through 18 months showed no degradation product increase or impurity change greater than 0.1 %.

1.1.1 Importance assessment for CP-4 material attributes

Fate and purge of related substances in CP-4 in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance is shown in the figure below.

CP-4 and CP-6 have tested positive in the Ames Assay. The intermediate CP-5 and intermediate precursor CP-3 exhibited positive structural alerts in a structure activity relationship database, therefore will be controlled as potentially mutagenic impurities (CP-4 and CP-6) as well.

Figure 1‑1      Fate and Purge of Related Substances in CP-4 in the Manufacturing Process of Sakuramil

1.1.2 Control items for CP-4 high risk material attributes:

CP-4 is designated a high risk material attribute and the specification is established at NMT 0.3 % in the intermediate specification of CP-6. CP-4 is one of the four potentially mutagenic impurities in the process to manufacture Sakuramil drug substance; and all four of these impurities will be controlled in either the API specification or SM/Intermediate specification. It should be noted that CP-5 and CP-3 (two other potentially mutagenic impurities) are controlled under the unspecified impurity specification as NMT 0.1 % in CP-6 as shown in the table above. However, even at this level of 0.1 % for each of these two impurities, the level in Sakuramil drug substance for CP-5 and CP-3 is typically seen well below 1 ppm combined. The reactivity of the functional center responsible for the potentially mutagenic activity (aniline) combined with the purge factors for these two impurities is 100 times greater than in CP-4. In addition, 37.5 ppm was chosen as a target in Sakuramil drug substance based on the additive effect and combined control strategy for the last potentially mutagenic impurity: CP-6. This upstream critical control point for CP-4 is part of the combined control for all potentially mutagenic impurities as summarized below.

Summary of Potentially mutagenic Control Strategy

Control Strategy for CP-4, CP-5, CP-3:

In CP-6: Important MA CP-4 (≤ 0.3 %) + CP-5 and CP-3 (≤ 0.1 % each) = ≤ 10 ppm total for these three in Sakuramil drug substance as demonstrated by risk assessment outlined here [[2 Risk Assessment]] and supported by carry over studies in section [[ICH M7 Risk Assessment]].

Control Strategy for CP-6 (Intermediate):

< 10 ppm in Sakuramil when process through Steps 3 & 4 design space (specification for CP-6 as a CQA in Sakuramil drug substance: ≤ 25 ppm)

Therefore: CP-3 is controlled in CP-4 Starting Material specification, CP-4 is controlled in CP-6 Intermediate specification and CP-5 is controlled as unspecified impurity in CP-6 Intermediate specification as per Option 3. CP-6 is controlled in drug substance specification as per Option 1. Therefore it is ensured that all potentially mutagenic impurities are well controlled in accordance with ICH M7.

1.1.3 Control items for CP-4 moderate risk material attributes:

Identity, assay, unspecified impurities, and total impurities have not been identified as important material attributes.

However, they are important when managing current suppliers or evaluating additional supplier of CP-4. 1.1.4 Control items for CP-4 low risk material attributes:

The enantiomer (CP-4-E) is a low risk material attribute. As discussed above, chirality is controlled in the CP-2 and the process and intermediates have no impact on the chiral control. In addition, the process has significant purge of all isomers as well as methods that are specific for, and confirmed, the correct enantiomer of Sakuramil (specifications for intermediate and the drug substance are specific for all chiral isomers). Manufacturing of the enantiomer would therefore not go undetected early in the process. Nevertheless, enantiomeric purity is controlled within CP-4 specification as it is the next step after introduction of the “chiral pool” of CP-2.

1.2 Starting Material 2 - CP-8

While the starting material CP-8 exhibited positive structural alerts in a structure activity relationship database, it was determined to be negative in the Ames assay. The Ames report is attached in 3.2.DS.C. Therefore, CP-8 is controlled in Sakuramil drug substance as an unspecified impurity with a limit of NMT 0.10%.

CP-8 has been manufactured by IROHA-corp. (China) and abcr Gmbh. (Germany) using the same manufacturing processes. CP-8 manufactured at commercial scale has been converted to Sakuramil drug substance that has been used in Phase 3 clinical trials and ICH drug substance stability studies.

The quality of CP-8 is tightly controlled in accordance with the commercial specification in section [[2.3.3.SM.C Control [CP-8] [Sakuramil]]]

Justification for section of CP-8 Starting Material is provided in section [[2.3.4.SM.D Description [CP-8][Sakuramil]]]

2.2.1 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Related substances

The following figure shows the impurities deriving from the manufacturing steps which could highly potentially impact CQA of Sakuramil. In step 3, ethyl homolog CP-7-1, the single impurity in the entire manufacturing process, is formed. CP-7-1 reacts and it converted to CP-9-1 in Step 4 and ultimately remains in the drug substance. CP-9-1 has very little purge in the crystallization in Step 4. Therefore, it is required to identify the process parameters which impact the formation and purge of CP-7-1 in Step 3.

In Step 4, unreacted SM CP-8 remains in the drug substance. Therefore, it is required to identify the process parameters which impact the formation and purge of CP-8 in Step 4.

SM CP-4, a potentially mutagenic impurity used in Step 1, is discussed in the section for potentially mutagenic impurities.

2.2.2 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Potentially mutagenic Impurities

SM CP-4, and CP-3, CP-5 and CP-6, potential impurities in SM, are potentially mutagenic impurities. It is required to investigate the process parameters which impact the purge of these impurities.

2.2.3 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Nitrosamine Impurities

Vulnerable amines are present in the drug substance, therefore it is required to investigate the risk on formation of N-nitrosamines. Nitrosating agents are not likely to be present in the drug substance.

2.2.4 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Chirality (Stereoisomers)

As stated in 1.2.6, no racemization has been observed in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance. As chirality is controlled in accordance with the vendor specifications of CP-2 as well as in the specifications of SM CP-4, and the manufacturing process and intermediates do not impact the control of chirality, it is not an important MA.

2.2.5 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Residual Solvents

Class 2 solvents THF, Methanol and n-Hexane are used in the manufacturing process, but because of several solid-liquid separation operations in the crystallization in Step 3 and Step 4, these solvents have not been detected in the development stage.

A Class 2 solvent dichloromethane is used in the reaction step in Step 4, but as it is designated to be submitted for crystallization after dichloromethane is evaporated after completion of the reaction, dichloromethane also has not been detected in the development stage. Therefore, it is not considered an important MA.

A Class 3 solvent Ethanol is used in all of the manufacturing steps (except Step 1) and it is defined a critical parameter as the content of Ethanol may influences the formation of ethyl homolog impurity (CP-7-1).

2.2.6 Material Attribute (MA) to be evaluated: Elemental impurities

Pd catalyst is used in the manufacturing process of the SM CP-4 in Step A. Therefore, Pd content has been included in the specification for SM as well as intermediate CP-6. As the level of metal does not increase in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance, it does not need to be controlled in final drug substance, however it is considered a important MA.

3 Design Space Development

For the purposes of defining the design space for the Sakuramil manufacturing process, the impact of the process on the critical quality attributes of Sakuramil was investigated in combination with quality risk management processes and tools. A design space for the commercial manufacture of Sakuramil has been established relative to its critical quality attributes and critical process inputs (material and process parameters). As there are no critical parameters in Step 1 and Step 2 that would not result in critical parameters in the final steps 3 and 4, this Design Spaces focuses on the final steps.

The following sections (Step 3 to Step 4) provide a summary of the risk based assessment of each step, the experimental work conducted, an assessment of the results and the resultant design space for each step, leading to the overall design space for the manufacturing process.

3.1 Focus area multivariate protocols, experimental summaries, and conclusions that set up the Design Space for Sakuramil drug substance

Introduction

Once the commercial route to Sakuramil was. established as described in the process development history section above, a greater understanding of the functional interrelationships of the manufacturing process parameters on the critical quality attributes of the dt.ug substance was established and this ultimately led to definition of the design space for the manufacturing process.

Initially, a risk assessment process was undertaken to identify all process parameters (including MA and in-process controls) and assess their probable impact on drug substance quality. In order to do this, each step of the manufacturing process was divided into focus areas (FA) and evaluated individually. Step 3 and Step 4 were each divided into FA1 - FA6. Evaluated FA are shown in Table 1-5. This initial risk assessment was conducted by means of Cause and Effect (C&E) Matrix. Examples of process parameters assessed are shown in Table 1-6.

First, the material attributes of the product for each step were assessed against their potential to impact a critical quality attribute of the dt.ug substance. Next, process parameters for each step were assessed against their potential to impact the important material att1·ibutes for that step product. The evaluation points were calculated and risks were classified into three levels (high, medium and low). This initial structured risk assessment utilized the knowledge that had been gained through development and scale up of the manufacturing process, and a mechanistic understanding of the chemistry of reactions and work up procedures.

The quality attributes that gain the highest priority to evaluate were the impurities generated and controlled by the process.

Scale and equipment consideration: (Prior to multivariate design to establish the design space)

As with many phase transfer reactions, the reaction rate will be severely impacted if the aqueous and organic phases are not adequately dispersed; however, product purity does not appear to suffer even after 24 hours under poor mixing conditions, indicating that the reaction is robust enough to withstand any mixing issues that may be encountered on scale ( e.g. temporary loss of agitation).

As expected, mixing has a very strong influence upon the rate of the phase transfer reaction, which proceeds faster at higher agitation speeds. If adequate dispersion of the aqueous and organic phases is not achieved, as was the case at 200 rpm in this series of experiments, the reaction may not be complete even after 24 hours. Even though only 70% conversion was reached after 24 hours at 200 rpm, reaction completion was achieved in 1.5 hours after increasing the agitation rate to disperse the phases.

Despite these results, the reaction appears robust enough such that in all of the experiments, product purity profiles were typical for all of the complete reactions, and issues with purity related to mixing are not anticipated upon scale-up.

Continued stressing experiments were executed to understand if there is any impact on prolonged time difference between laboratory and manufacturing times on the quality attributes. 3.2.DS.M.5 Changes during development

Development History

1 Route A: First Generation Synthesis

Figure 1‑1      Route A: First Generation Synthesis

• Disadvantages

• Resolution discards 50% of the wrong enantiomer: not reasonable for high volume products

• Safety: Use of hazardous reagents/chemistry

• Trifluromethylbromoaniline (potential HF generation)

• N-vinylcarbamate (polymerizes and generates impurity)

• Azide chemistry (explosive)

• Suppliers for this route are limited due to the hazards associated to this chemistry

2 Route B: Second Generation Synthesis

Figure 1‑2      Route B: Second Generation Synthesis

Improvements from Route A

• Use safer and reliable technology that reduces the use of hazardous reagents

• Elimination of resolution step

• Technology that can be nm in a general 1m1pose plants

• More efficient capacity utilization for large volume product

• Multiple vendors and the supplier option

Process highlights that needed to be addressed for commercialization

• Step CP-6 to CP-7

• Reaction done in DCM with IPE as the isolation solvent

• Pyridine use as base for the reaction with ethyl chloroformate

• Reaction done at a low temperature to reduce decomposition

• Reaction typically resulted in 2% unreacted starting material

• Step CP-7 to Sakuramil

• Potassium t-butoxide reacts with methylene chloride when CP-7 is absent, potential safety issue identified.

• Potassium t-butoxide must be titrated to reaction to avoid fo1mation of impurities difficult to purge

• Two solid charges / worker exposure potential.

• Large volumes of DCM also needled

• The process requires a significant excess of CP-8 (1 .4 eq.) an expensive reagent classified as a sensitizer (P-4).

• The reaction typically leaves 1 to 2.5% of starting material

3 Route C: Third Generation Synthesis

Figure 1‑3      Route C: Third Generation Synthesis

Key Improvements to Commercial Process

• Step CP-6 to CP-7

• Reaction done in THF with Ethanol/water as the isolation solvent

• Pyridine was substituted by sodium carbonate

• No stability issue

• Reaction typically resulted in ≤ 0.5 % unreacted starting material

• Step CP-7 to Sakuramil

• Reaction is done using 50% NaOH and a phase transfer catalyst

• DCM still needed but with significantly volumes reductions

• No stability or incompatibility issues between reagents/solvents

• The process requires only 1.03 equiv of CP-8 (vs. 1.4 eq. Old process) an expensive reagent classified as a sensitizer (P-4).

• The reaction typically leaves ~ 0.5% of starting material

3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Residual Solvents) [Residual Solvents][Sakuramil][CP-4]

3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description

Analytical method is performed in-line with USP <467> Procedure A, compendial GC method.

3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

For the determination of residual solvents, a compendial GC method (USP <467> Procedure A) is used. The method is verified in accordance with USP <1467> Residual Solvents – Verification of compendial procedures and validation of alternative procedures. Verification of compendial methods for limit tests like Residual solvents includes the parameters specificity, detection limit (LOD) and solution stability.

2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary

In the present report, verification results of the determination of residual solvents test (GC) as described in USP <467> Procedure A are compiled and evaluated.

The method considers the specified residual solvent from Sakuramil drug substance. Specified residual solvent as per DMF section [[2.3.3.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] is Dichloromethane. Additionally, the method is used for determination of the IPC Ethanol (IPC #2).

The analytical procedure can be stated validated in accordance with ICH Q2(R2) and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

For determination of residual solvents by GC, specificity, limit of detection (LOD) and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to USP <1467> Residual Solvents—Verification of Compendial Procedures and Validation of Alternative Procedures and current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures. USP <1467> is focusing on Class 1 and 2 solvents, however, the same procedure was applied for Ethanol determination in order to ensure that the method is suitable under actual conditions of use.

Following acceptance criteria have been defined in a method verification protocol.

Table 2‑1 Acceptance criteria

Verification ParameterAcceptance CriteriaResults
Specificity / System Suitability Requirements· Reagent blank does not produce any significant interference with any of the other peaks from solvents Dichloromethane and Ethanol. · Separation of the solvent peaks in the standard solution from other peaks in the spiked sample solution (Resolution: NLT 1.0).Resolution standard solution: Dimethylformamide / Dichloromethane = 9.9 Dimethylformamide / Ethanol = 6.4 Ethanol / Dichloromethane = 5.8 Spiked sample solution: Dimethylformamide / Dichloromethane = 10.1 Dimethylformamide / Ethanol = 6.3 Ethanol / Dichloromethane = 5.8
Limit of Detection (LOD)S/N ≥ 3 (n = NLT 3)LOD = 6 ppm
Stability of SolutionsDetection limit for limit tests should be met throughout the testing periodFor the spiked sample solution #B221157 the respective acceptance criteria of relative change are fulfilled for 28 hours for Dichloromethane and Ethanol. Standard solution: During the tested time period the relative change of Dichloromethane and Ethanol peak areas is within respective acceptance criterion (≤ 10 % relative change with respect to initial).

Evaluation of the results confirmed that the GC method is suitable for determination of the residual solvents in Sakuramil drug substance tested at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Verification parameters specificity and limit of detection (LOD) fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.

Additionally, the stability of standard solution and test solution stored in the autosampler at RT (25°C) have been demonstrated. A holdup time of at least 28 hours was defined for both standard and test solution.

Evaluation of the results confirmed that the GC method used for determination of residual solvents Dichloromethane and IPC Ethanol in Sakuramil is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Verification parameter specificity and limit of detection (LOD) fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.

The analytical procedure can be stated validated and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

2.3.4.SM.D Description [CP-4][Sakuramil][CP-6]

Reasons for designating CP-4 as regulatory starting material in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil are as follows:

• CP-4 is a significant structural fragment incorporated in the structure of the Sakuramil drug substance.

CP-4 contains the main core structure of Sakuramil: one of the trifluoromethyl as well as the amine residues.

• It is a substance of defined chemical properties and structure.

• CP-4 can be considered as “custom synthesized chemicals” according to ICH Q11 and ICH Q11 Q&A guideline principles.

• Specifications of starting material CP-4 has been well defined to ensure adequate quality of starting material used in the synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance (refer to [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] ).

• Discussion on potential impurities of CP-4, their origin as well as fate and purge are presented within [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]].

• Multiple chemical transformation steps are available between CP-4 and final drug substance.

• In line with all general principles of ICH guideline Q11 on development and manufacture of drug substances (chemical entities and biotechnological/biological entities) and Q&A document.

2.3.4.SM.M Manufacture [CP-4][Sakuramil][CP-6]

Manufacturing process (CP-4)

Figure 1-1           Reaction scheme (CP-4, IROHA-corp.)

4-Brom-benzotrifluorid (CP-1) reacts with (3R)-3-Aminohexanenitrile (CP-2) to form in situ intermediate CP-3 in presence of Pd catalyst/ligand as well as base and toluene (Step A). In Step B, Starting Material CP-4 is formed by reacting with concentrated sulphuric acid solution, toluene and heptane.

Figure 1-2           Reaction scheme (CP-4, HETO-corp.)

4-Brom-benzotrifluorid (CP-1) reacts with (3R)-3-Aminohexanenitrile (CP-2) to form CP-3 in presence of Pd catalyst as well as ligand and toluene during temperature heating up to 70°C. In the next step, Starting Material CP-4 is formed by reacting with concentrated sulphuric acid solution and toluene.

2.3.4.SM.D Description [CP-8][Sakuramil]

Reasons for designating CP-8 as regulatory starting material in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil are as follows:

• CP-8 is a significant structural fragment incorporated in the structure of the Sakuramil drug substance.

CP-8 is a bis-trifluoromethyl benzene side chain incorporated in the structure of the Sakuramil.

• It is a substance of defined chemical properties and structure.

• Starting material CP-8 can be “custom synthesized chemicals” according to ICH Q11 and ICH Q11 Q&A guideline principles.

• Specifications of starting material CP-8 has been well defined to ensure adequate quality of starting materials used in the synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance (refer to [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] ).

• Discussion on potential impurities of CP-8, their origin as well as fate and purge are presented within [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]]

Impurities that are defined to impact the impurity profile of Sakuramil do not originate from earlier steps than of the starting materials. Manufacturing steps upstream of CP-8 are simple.

• Only one chemical transformation step is available between CP-8 and final drug substance. CP-8 is controlled in the drug substance to the level of NMT 0.10%.

• In line with all general principles of ICH guideline Q11 on development and manufacture of drug substances (chemical entities and biotechnological/biological entities) and Q&A document.

2.3.4.SM.M Manufacture [CP-8][Sakuramil]

Manufacturing process (CP-8)

Figure 1-1         Reaction scheme (CP-8)

3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)benzaldehyde is reacted with NaBH4 in ethanol to form the intermediate (3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)phenyl)methanol CP-8-OH. The intermediate is then brominated with HBr/H2SO4 to form 3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)benzyl bromide.

1.2.1 STAGE 1 – SELECTION OF SYNTHETIC ROUTE

Selection of the appropriate synthetic route was based on available literature data. The first goal was to select appropriate synthetic route, starting materials and raw materials which would enable the synthesis the targeted molecule.

Full details on changes during development can be found in section  2.3.4.DS.M.2 Changes during manufacturing process development

1.2.2.1 Definition of Raw Materials, Reagents and Starting Materials

1.2.2.1.1 Starting Materials

IROHA-corp. proposed that CP-4 and CP-8 serve as structurally distinct and suitable Starting Materials (SM), or “Regulatory Starting Materials” (RSM). The proposed “Regulatory Synthesis” is convergent, consisting of four synthetic steps, wherein significant molecular fragments are incorporated to create Sakuramil drug substance. The proposed “Regulatory Synthesis” was selected extensive based on laboratory and manufacturing experience established a high degree of process understanding. The appropriate specifications for SMs have been established to assure the quality of Sakuramil drug substance.

CP-4 that was manufactured by the three development routes, as outlined in section , have all produced Sakuramil drug substances that meet the current specifications. In addition, batches of CP-4 have been manufactured by a second supplier using second and third generation synthesis. All of these resulted in CP-4 and Sakuramil drug substance with similar impurity profiles and of high quality. There were not any impurities from all of these batches or route modifications of CP4  that resulted in any impurity above the 0.15 % level in Sakuramil drug substance. The potentially mutagenic impurity CP-3, originating from CP-4 synthesis, controlled at NMT 0.3% in CP-4 was shown to be purged in the drug substance to

CP-4 tested positive in the Ames assay classified as potentially mutagenic impurities. CP-3, although not directly tested, exhibited structural alerts in SAR databases and is therefore also controlled as potentially mutagenic. Fate and purge studies confirmed that CP-4 and CP-3 are effectively removed during the manufacturing process, resulting in levels 10% below TTC (37.5 ppm) in the final drug substance Both impurities are controlled upstream on suitable intermediate with limit above TTC. Option 3 per ICH M7 guideline is used. These findings support the adequacy of the control strategy and justify the use of CP-4 as a suitable starting material.

1.2.2 STAGE 2 – LABORATORY SCALE PROCESS DEVELOPMENT

Initial experiments in Stage 2 were oriented towards getting scientifically sound understanding of mechanistic background synthesize and isolation. The process was then optimized and the parameters evaluated on a laboratory scale. Parameters were generally varied to an extent sufficient to determine the proven acceptable ranges. Design of experiments (DoE) was used to build a model of operation and gain specific knowledge about the parameters affecting attributes which are important for process performance and quality of the product. The product isolation was also developed at this stage.

1.2.3 STAGE 3 – MANUFACTURING PROCESS SCALE UP, DRYING STEP OPTIMIZATION AND PRODUCTION OF DEVELOPMENT AND PRODUCTION BATCHES

After the laboratory development, where small scale laboratory process was confirmed, further development work was focused on commercial manufacturing process.

The process designed at the laboratory level was adjusted to the specific manufacturing equipment. Adjustment of the process demanded the redefinition and optimization of some process parameters, since some operations are scale and equipment dependent. Scale up effects and data required to define equipment and to set parameters for successful transfer from laboratory to industrial scale were identified.

Commercial Manufacturing Process is outlined in section [[2.3.3.DS.M Manufacture (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]]

2 Risk Assessment

Once the commercial manufacturing process for Sakuramil drug substance was established, increased understanding of the functional relationships between manufacturing process inputs (raw materials, SM, intermediates, etc.) and operating parameters (and their respective levels of criticality) and critical quality attributes of the drug substance was developed. This ultimately led to defining a design space and a control strategy for the manufacturing process.

Initially, a risk assessment process was undertaken to identify potentially critical process parameters and potential scale and equipment dependencies and assess their probable impact on drug substance quality (resulting in an understanding of their criticality and definition of inputs and operating parameters as high risk (critical), moderate risk (key) or low risk (non-critical)). In this risk assessment process, each step of the manufacturing process was considered individually. Firstly, the material attributes of the product for each step were considered with respect to their potential to impact a critical quality attribute of the drug substance. For drug substance processes, this is strictly an impurity exercise until the isolation of the drug substance, where physical characteristic are included. Next, process inputs and process operating parameters for each step were assessed with respect to their potential to impact the important impurity attributes for that step in the process.

This initial structured risk assessment utilized the knowledge that had been gained through development and scale up of the manufacturing process, and a mechanistic and kinetic understanding of the chemistry and the manufacturing process. After identifying the process inputs (raw materials, SM, intermediates, etc.) and process operating parameters and their potential links to drug substance critical quality attributes, an experimental plan was developed, prioritized and executed in order to (a) establish if the identified parameter does impact the quality attributes, and (b) to determine the extent of this impact and identify the design space / proven acceptable ranges (PAR) within which the process can be operated to produce drug substance that meets its specification.

All process-related impurities, including intermediates, diastereomers, and potentially mutagenic compounds, have been identified and assessed throughout the commercial manufacturing process of Sakuramil. CP-6 impurities above 0.1% are controlled based on demonstrated purge capability, and unspecified impurities are limited to NMT 0.1%. The process consistently achieves the desired impurity profile through robust crystallizations, which efficiently purge lipophilic intermediates and impurities.

Key material attributes impacting CQAs include:

• CP-7-1 and CP-9-1, formed in Steps 3 and 4, with low purge and controlled via process parameters.

• Unreacted CP-8, retained in the drug substance, requiring control in Step 4.

• Potentially mutagenic impurities (CP-3, CP-4, CP-5, CP-6) are purged below TTC levels.

• Nitrosamine risk is low due to absence of nitrosating agents, though vulnerable amines are present.

• Chirality is not impacted by the process and remains controlled.

• Residual solvents are effectively removed during crystallization.

• Elemental impurities, such as Pd, are controlled at the SM and intermediate level, with no need for control in the final drug substance.

Full details on commercial manufacturing process related impurities [[3.2.DS.M.2 Development of manufacturing process and process control]]

3 Description of Critical Material Attributes and Critical Process Parameters

3.1 Design space development

A comprehensive design space was established for the Sakuramil manufacturing process based on risk assessments, multivariate experiments, and mechanistic understanding. Focus was placed on Steps 3 and 4, where critical quality attributes (CQAs) are most impacted.

Equivalents (2.0–7.5), sodium carbonate stoichiometry (0.75–4.0), and THF volume (3–15 L/kg), along with crystallization parameters such as cooling rate (0.15–0.5 °C/min), water content (10–50% w/w), ethanol volume (4–10 L/kg), and agitation rate. CP-7-1 remained below the 0.15% specification in all tested conditions, with no edges of failure observed.

In Step 4, residual CP-8 was the primary concern. DoE variables included CP-8 stoichiometry (0.9–2.0 equivalents), phase ratio (NaOH/DCM, 0.25–1.25), reaction concentration (0.25–5 L/kg), cooling rate (0.15–0.5 °C/min), and water content (20–35% w/w). Cooling rate and water content were identified as critical process parameters (CPPs), and when controlled, CP-8 levels remained below 0.10% in the drug substance. Overall, the design space ensures robust control of impurities for Sakuramil drug substance. Further Information on design space development is provided in section [[3 Design Space Development]].

4 Drug Substance CQAs

Based upon knowledge of the product (QTPP and CQA for drug product) and the process, several drug substance critical quality attributes (CQAs) were proposed. The links between drug substance CQAs on the one hand and critical process parameters (CPPs) and critical material attributes (CMAs) on the other hand were established.

4.1 Drug Substance Critical Quality Attributes

Critical Quality Attributes of Sakuramil Drug substance are: Identification, Assay, Purity Related substances, Purity Potentially mutagentic impurities, Purity Residual solvents, Purity Elemental impurities, as outlined in table below.

Table 2-1 Critical and Non-Critical Quality Attributes for Sakuramil

Quality AttributeTestsCriticalityRationale
DescriptionDescriptionNot criticalICH Q6A, Universal test
IdentificationIR, HPLCCriticalICH Q6A, Universal test
PotencyAssayCriticalICH Q6A Decision Tree #5, Universal test
PurityRelated substancesCriticalICH Q6A Decision Tree #1, Universal test
PurityPotentially mutagenic impuritiesCriticalPotentially mutagenic impurities have been identified.
PurityNitrosamine impuritiesNot CriticalNitrosamine Risk Assessment provided evidence that there is no risk on formation of N-nitrosamine.
PurityResidual solventsCriticalClass 2 and class 3 solvents are used in the manufacturing process.
PurityElemental impuritiesCriticalPd catalyst is used in the manufacturing process of SM1 (CP-4)
PurityResidue on ignitionNot criticalPharmacopeial test
Physicochemical propertyMelting pointNot criticalNo polymorphs have been observed
Particle size/Not criticalICH Q6A Decision Tree #3: It is considered not critical for the drug substance quality; however, the drug product manufacturing is based on wet-granulation, it is classified as critical for the drug product. Setting acceptance criteria is based on drug product development.
Polymorphism/Not criticalICH Q6A Decision Tree #4: It is considered not critical for the drug substance quality; polymorphism screening has been conducted on drug substance, and drug product level. No different polyforms have been formed.
Optical activityStereoisomersNot criticalICH Q6A Decision Tree #5SM1 is optically-active substance. Stereoisomers are controlled in CP-4 specification.
Water contentLoss on dryingNot criticalSakuramil drug substance shows no hygroscopic property.
Microbial limit/Not criticalICH Q6A Decision Tree #6Sakuramil drug substance is not capable of supporting microbial growth or viability. It is classified as critical for the drug product, therefore controlled in drug porduct specification.

The synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance was evaluated regarding the manufacturing process impact on impurity control. Therefore, CQA of Sakuramil can be controlled by understanding and controlling the formation routes and fate and purge of impurities. The following related substances are found necessary to be controlled in Sakuramil drug substance specification: CP-9-1 with limit NMT 0.15% and CP-8 with limit of NMT 0.10%, meanwhile Individual unspecified impurities are limited at NMT 0.10%.

The identification and control of potentially mutagenic impurities were done according to ICH M7 guideline. An in silico assessment was performed using DEREK Nexus and SARAH Nexus. The following impurities are found to be potentially mutagenic and control strategy was appropriately established in line with control options per ICH M7 guideline.

CP-3, originating from SM CP-4, Class 3, Controlled as per ICH M7 Option 3; CP-3 is included in CP-4 specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%. Carry over results on three final API batches demonstrate levels of CP-3 below 30% of TTC.

CP-4, SM, Class 3, controlled as per ICH M7 Option 3; CP-4 is included in CP-6 specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%. Carry over results on three final API batches demonstrate levels of CP-4 below 30% of TTC.

CP-5, API synthesis, Class 3, controlled as per ICH M7 Option 3; Residual CP-5 is monitored and controlled as Individual unspecified impurity within intermediate CP-6 specification with a limit of NMT 0.1%. Carry over results on three final API batches demonstrate levels of CP-4 below 30% of TTC.

CP-6, API synthesis, Class 3, controlled as per ICH M7 Option 1; included  in Sakuramil drug substance specification with limit of NMT 37.5 ppm

For further details on ICH M7 assessment, please refer to [[ICH M7 Risk Assessment]].

Solvents used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance are the following : methyl chloroformate, tetrahydrofuran, methanol, ethanol, n-hexane, methylene chloride. Potential residual solvents originating from starting materials are the following: toluene, heptane.Dichloromethane is used in the last step of the synthesis of Sakuramil and only residual dichloromethane is routinely controlled in the drug substance specification with a limit of NMT 600 ppm per ICH Q3C guideline. For all other solvents (ethanol, methanol, n-hexane, tetrahydrofuran, benzene, toluene) carry over results on three API batches  are present demonstrating levels below 10% of the corresponding ICH Q3C limit.

In line with ICH Q3D Guideline for Elemental Impurities, the Risk Assessment was performed in order to identify known and potential sources of elemental impurities in Sakuramil drug substance.

No class 1 elements are intentionally used and hence, not likely to be present in Sakuramil drug substance. Palladium (Pd) – class 2B element - is intentionally added in manufacturing process of SM1 CP-4, controlled in CP4 specification with NMT 10 ppm and therefore also considered in the risk assessment. Lithium (Li) – class 3 element – is intentionally added in form of the reagent Lithium-tert-butoxide. Results of carry over studies according to ICH Q3D guideline are provided in [[2.3.4.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]].

Final manufacturing process that was used for non-clinical/clinical, registration and validation batches is outlined in section [[2.3.3.DS.M Manufacture (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]]

2.3.4.DS.M.3 Comparability for multiple manufacturing sites

There is only one commercial manufacturing site for Sakuramil, therefore this section is not applicable.

2.3.4.DS.M.4 Summary of process validation or evaluation studies

Sakuramil is a non-sterile molecule, therefore process validation data are not required to be provided at the time of application.

Routine reprocessing is not part of the manufacturing process.

Raw materials are not recycled and regenerated.

Manufacturing equipment is intend for reuse. All equipment undergoes validated cleaning processes. Cleaning validations in place demonstrates that the equipment can be safely reused without risk of cross-contamination. The equipment has a proven history of reliable performance across multiple campaigns, with no adverse impact on product quality or safety.

resource.title: Manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance (IROHA-corp.)
resource.description: Four-step synthesis CP-4 -> CP-5 (in situ) -> CP-6 -> CP-7 -> CP-9 (Sakuramil). Typical commercial batch size 350 kg.

action.title: Step 1
action.description: CP-4 is combined with methyl chloroformate, lithium-tert-butoxide, and tetrahydrofuran, then stirred. Layers are settled and separated. Precipitates are filtered, rinsed with tetrahydrofuran and dried to yield CP-5.

action.title: Step 2
action.description: CP-5 is combined with sodium borohydride, magnesium chloride, and methanol, then filtered after the reaction completes. Hydrochloric acid is added to the filtrate, layers are settled and separated. Organic layer is distilled with ethanol, and the mixture is stirred with water. Resulting precipitate is filtered, rinsed and dried to yield CP-6.

valueCodeableConcept.text: CPP #3.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

action.title: Step 3
action.description: CP-6 is combined with tetrahydrofuran, sodium carbonate, and ethyl chloroformate, then heated to reflux. Upon reaction completion, the mixture is filtered and quenched with sodium hydroxide, n-hexane is added, the layers are separated, and the organic layer is distilled with ethanol and stirred with water (CPP #3.1). After filtering and drying it results in CP-7.

action.title: CPP #3.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

extension.valueString: 98-105 L; then 20 to 35% w/w of ethanol

valueCodeableConcept.text: CPP #4.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

action.title: Step 4
action.description: CP-7 and CP-8 are combined in methylene chloride followed by the addition of tetra-n-butylammonium bromide and aqueous sodium hydroxide solution while mixing. Upon reaction completion, methylene chloride and water are added (CPP #4.1); ethanol content is monitored by IPC #1. The mixture is separated, washed, cooled (CPP #4.2, IPC #2) and concentrated with ethanol. After filtering and drying it results in CP-9 (Sakuramil).

action.title: CPP #4.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

2.3.4.DS.D Description (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]

The identity of the drug substance was confirmed using orthogonal analytical techniques, refer to a table 1-1 for an overview, each supporting the expected structural and physicochemical characteristics.

Table 1-1 Overview of original analytical techniques performed

Analytical techniquesConclusions based on batch #B221031Supporting informations
1H NMR spectrometryAssignments of H protons and 1H NMR spectrum is consistent with the proposed structure of Sakuramil drug substance structure[[1H Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR)]]
13C NMR spectrometryAssignments of Carbons and C13 NMR spectrum is consistent with the proposed structure of Sakuramil drug substance structure[[13C Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR)]]
IR spectroscopyThe IR spectrum of the sample is consistent with literature source. The IR spectrum shows characteristic absorption bands confirming the presence of functional groups such as hydroxyl (-OH), carboxylates, carbonyl (C=O), and various C-H and C-N. Characteristic absorption bands are present, confirming the identity of the drug substance.[[Infrared spectrometry (IR)]]
UV spectroscopyThe UV absorption spectrum of the sample exhibits characteristic maxima at 251 nm, consistent with the expected chromophoric features of the drug substance.[[Ultraviolet Spectroscopy (UV)]]
Mass spectrometryThe mass spectrum of the sample shows a molecular ion peak at m/z 614.504, which matches the theoretical molecular weight of the drug substance m/z 614.505. Additionally, the observed fragment ions correspond to the predicted fragmentation pattern based on the proposed structure.[[Mass spectrometry (MS)]]
Elemental analysisThe experimentally determined elemental composition (%C 52.78, %H 4.41, %F 27.81, %N 4.56) is consistent with the theoretical values calculated for the proposed molecular formula of the drug substance. All values fall within acceptable analytical tolerances, supporting the identity of the compound[[Elemental Analysis]]
X-ray powder diffraction (XRPD)The XRPD patterns of the test sample and the retained sample (24 month) show excellent agreement in both 2θ positions and relative intensities, indicating that the crystalline form of the drug substance has been preserved. XRPD analysis of Sakuramil across stability time points till end of Shelf-life (initial, 6 months, 24 months, 36 months) under ICH conditions (25°C/60% RH, and 40°C/75% RH) showed consistent diffraction peaks at 2θ values of 12.3°, 18.7°, 22.5°, and 27.1°,…… confirming the retention of the same crystalline polymorph. No peak shifts, broadening, or new peaks were observed, indicating polymorphic stability.[[Polymorphism (X-ray powder diffraction (XRPD)]]
pHpH of Sakuramil drug substance batch no. B221031 is: pH = 7.85 (0.12 g/ml, 20°C)-

ICH M7 Risk Assessment

1 Potentially mutagenic impurities – ICH M7 Risk Assessment

Risk Assessment has been carried out according to ICH M7 guideline including classification of impurities with respect to mutagenic and carcinogenic potential based on literature data or in silico (Q)SAR assessment of impurities (using DEREK Nexus, SARAH Nexus). Results are provided in table below.

CP-6 (including enantiomer and diastereomer) and CP-4 (including enantiomer) have been tested positive in both (Q)SAR systems. The intermediate CP-5 and precursor intermediate CP-3 (non-isolated intermediates) exhibit positive structural alerts in a structure activity relationship database with the same aniline functionality. However, due to design of the manufacturing synthesis, these three intermediated and CP-4 are reacted in Step 3 to eliminate the aniline functionality responsible for the potential mutagenic characteristics. The reactivity of these potentially mutagenic impurities and intermediates together with the hydrophobicity of formed CP-7 and CP-9 (Sakuramil), in addition to, the Steps 3 and 4 crystallizations have excellent purge of the resulting unreacted drug aniline and byproducts, have consistently enabled control of these potentially mutagenic impurities in Sakuramil drug substance to a total of four (CP-6, CP-5, CP-4 and CP-3) of ≤ 37.5 ppm (37.5 ppm is the concentration limit of potentially mutagenic impurities of Sakuramil based on the highest dose). Concentration limit is calculated by dividing TTC by Maximum daily dose. TTC value is 1.5 µg/day as per ICH M7 guideline. Maximum daily dose of Sakuramil is 40 mg (= 0.04 g).

The aniline group that is responsible for the mutagenicity is classified by IARC (International Agency for Research on Cancer) as Group 3 according to ICH M7 guideline with a lifetime permissible daily exposure (PDE) of 720 µg/day.

Solvents, inorganic acids or salts are not covered by this risk assessment as these are controlled by other ICH guidelines.

1.1 Methodology

Hazard assessment of impurities in the Sakuramil synthesis involved:

• Initial analysis of actual and potential impurities by conducting database and literature searches for carcinogenicity and bacterial mutagenicity data

• Classification of impurities with respect to mutagenic and carcinogenic potential based on literature data

• (Q)SAR assessment of impurities for which literature data are not available using

• DEREK Nexus (Lhasa Ltd.)

• SARAH Nexus (Lhasa Ltd.)

• Classification of impurities with respect to mutagenic and carcinogenic potential based on (Q)SAR predictions and expert knowledge

1.2 Classification of impurities

Classification of substances into classes as proposed by ICH M7: Assessment and control of DNA reactive (mutagenic) impurities in pharmaceuticals to limit potential carcinogenic risk.

Table 1-1 Classification of substances into classes

* or other relevant positive mutagenicity data indicative of DNA-reactivity related induction of gene mutations (e.g., positive findings in in vivo gene mutation studies)

1.3 Results of ICH M7 Risk Assessment

Table 1-2 Results of ICH M7 Risk Assessment

1.4 Rational for classification

Class 5 substances

Substances were shown to be negative for mutagenicity with both (Q)SAR systems. Based on the consensus (Q)SAR predictions, substances were deemed to lack mutagenic potential and were therefore considered as class 5 substances. For ethyl chloroformate and methyl chloroformate predictions to be negative for mutagenicity were used as a basis for classification.

Class 3 substances

Substances that were positive in both (Q)SAR systems. All of them containing an aniline group. As per Table for Classification of substances, Class 3 substances show alerting structure and are unrelated to the structure of the drug substance.

2 Control Strategy

All of these substances are controlled either within Sakuramil drug substance specification, Starting Material CP-4 specification or Intermediate CP-6 specification.

CP-3 is controlled in CP-4 Starting Material specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%, CP-4 is controlled in CP-6 Intermediate specification with a limit of NMT 0.3%, CP-5 is controlled as unspecified impurity in CP-6 Intermediate specification with a limit of NMT 0.1% as per Option 3 and CP-6 is controlled in the active substance specification with a limit of NMT 37.5 ppm as per Option 1. Therefore it is ensured that all potentially mutagenic impurities are well controlled in accordance with ICH M7.

Nitrosamine Risk Assessment

The Risk Assessment considers the potential presence of nitrosamine impurities in Sakuramil drug substance based on the manufacturing process as defined in section [[2.3.3.DS.M Manufacture (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]].

The risk evaluation is performed using quality risk management principles, as outlined in ICH Q9 Quality Risk Management guideline.

The risk assessment has evaluated the following items as potential sources of nitrosamines or their precursors in line with root causes described in EMA/409815/2020.

Risk factors related to the manufacture of the active substance:

• Use of nitrite salts and esters (e.g. NaNO2, alkyl nitrites), or other nitrosating agents (e.g. nitroso halides, nitrosonium salts, nitrogen oxides, nitro alkanes, halogenated nitro alkanes, Fremy’s salt, nitroso sulfonamides), in the presence of secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process. Sources for secondary or tertiary amines can also be starting materials, intermediates, reagents, solvents (e.g. DMF, DMAc and NMP) and catalysts, which contain amine functionality, amine impurities (e.g. quaternary ammonium salts) or which are susceptible to degradation to reveal amines.

• Nitrite formation by oxidation of hydroxylamine or nitrite release from nitro-aromatic precursors (e.g. by fluoro de-nitration), in the presence of secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process.

• Use of disinfected water (chlorination, chloro-amination, ozonisation) in the presence secondary or tertiary amines within the same or different steps of the manufacturing process.

• Oxidation of hydrazines, hydrazides and hydrazones by hypochlorite, air, oxygen, ozone and peroxides in the manufacturing process or during storage

• Use of contaminated raw, recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) in the API manufacturing process.

• Use of contaminated starting materials and intermediates supplied by vendors who use processes or raw materials which may contain residual nitrosamines or nitrosating agents.

• Carry-over of nitrosamines deliberately generated (e.g. as starting materials or intermediates) during the manufacturing process.

Risk factors also related to finished product:

• A particular risk of formation of nitrosamines should be noted for active substances that contain a nitrosatable amine functional group. Several examples have been reported where the amine functionality was shown to be vulnerable to nitrosation and formation of the corresponding N-nitroso impurity (i.e. NO-API). Secondary amines appear particularly vulnerable to this reaction, although some cases with tertiary amines have also been observed.

• Does the API, or one of its known impurities, have a nitrosatable nitrogen functionality?

• May nitrites be present in one of the used excipients?

• Degradation processes of active substances, including those induced by inherent reactivity (e.g. presence of nitro-alkyl, oxime, or other functionality) or by the presence of an exogenous nitrosating agent.

• Oxidation of hydrazine or other amine-containing functional groups present in active substances or their impurities/degradants (e.g. from hydrazones and hydrazides), either in active substance manufacturing processes or during storage.

• Use of certain packaging materials.

• Reaction of amines leaching from quaternary ammonium anion exchange resins (e.g. used for purification steps) with nitrosating agents present in the liquid phase. In addition, disinfection procedures such as e.g. chlorination, chloro-amination and ozonisation can lead to significant N-nitrosamine generation as by-products in case vulnerable amines are present. Given the source of contamination, risk is related to the concentration of the reactive agent(s) and thus, to the volume of water in or used to dilute a particular product. The same risks could be associated with active substances or finished products manufactured using water purified using similar resins.

Risk factors related to GMP aspects:

• Cross-contamination due to different processes being run successively on the same manufacturing line.

• Carry-over of impurities between process steps due to operator-related errors or insufficiently detailed batch records such as inadequate phase separations during work-up procedures.

• Use of contaminated recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) where the recovery is outsourced to third parties who are not aware of the content of the materials they are processing. Recovery processes carried out in non-dedicated equipment should also be considered.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?

■ Yes

Justification:

The following starting materials are used in the manufacturing process: SM1 CP4 and SM2 CP-8. Sodium nitrite is used in the synthesis of SM2 CP-8 (1-bromo-3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)benzene) as indicated by the route of synthesis of that Starting Material below.

In the proposed manufacturing process of SM2 CP-8 (1-bromo-3,5-bis(trifluoromethyl)benzene) is prepared in a two-step synthesis starting from Br2. In the second step NaNO2 is used as a reagent to generate CP-8 from the intermediate 2-bromo-4-fluoroaniline HBr. The manufacturer from CP-8 Starting Material confirmed that vulnerable amines and vulnerable amine precursors are not used in the SM2 synthesis, therefore the risk for formation of N-nitrosamines and contamination of SM2 with nitrosamines is negligible. Nevertheless, since sodium nitrite is used it has to be assessed if some residual nitrite might be present in SM2 CP-8 and carried over into the Sakuramil drug substance manufacturing process. Considering the route of synthesis, there is no secondary or tertiary amine to form N-nitrosamine impurities in presence of sodium nitrite. Primary amines like the intermediate 2-bromo-4-fluoroaniline HBr are not capable of formation of N-nitrosamine in presence of sodium nitrite. Furthermore, considering the route of synthesis of Sakuramil drug substance after introduction of CP-8 (Step 4), there is a basic condition at low temperature of 12-25 °C. Both conditions do not support formation of N-nitrosamine impurities. Therefore, the overall risk is for formation/presence of nitrosamines due to SM2 CP-8 is evaluated as negligible.

SM 1 CP-4 contains vulnerable amine. As there is no source of nitrites in Step 1 of Sakuramil manufacturing process there is no risk for formation of corresponding nitrosamine. However, in step 2 CP-5 intermediate, containing vulnerable amine moiety, is converted to CP-6 (also vulnerable amine). In this stage water is used under acidic conditions therefore risk for formation of the corresponding nitrosamines from CP-5 and CP-6 can not be fully excluded. Nevertheless, it is expected that potential nitrosamine of CP-5 would be converted during Step 2 to nitrosamine of CP-6. Therefore, it can be assumed that the levels of nitroso-CP-6, if present, would be significantly higher, than the levels of nitroso-CP-5 and therefore, only nitroso-CP-6 is relevant for further mitigation.

In conclusion, there is a potential risk for nitroso-CP-6 formation in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance, therefore testing of final drug substance batches is needed.

Justification: N-nitrosamines are not deliberately generated during the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance. Therefore, the risk for the formation of nitrosamines due to this root cause is considered as not applicable.

Risk factors also related to the finished product

8 A particular risk of formation of nitrosamines should be noted for active substances that contain a nitrosatable amine functional group. Several examples have been reported where the amine functionality was shown to be vulnerable to nitrosation and formation of the corresponding N-nitroso impurity (i.e. NO-API). Secondary amines appear particularly vulnerable to this reaction, although some cases with tertiary amines have also been observed.
8a Does the API, or one of its known impurities, have a nitrosatable nitrogen functionality?

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?

□ Yes

■ No

□ N.A.

Justification: Sakuramil drug substance does not contain vulnerable/nitrosatable amine functionality.

8b May nitrites be present in one of the used excipients?

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines identified?

■ N.A.

Justification: N/A. This should be evaluated by DP manufacturer.

9 Degradation processes of active substances, including those induced by inherent reactivity (e.g. presence of nitro-alkyl, oxime, or other functionality) or by the presence of an exogenous nitrosating agent.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

■ N.A.

Justification: Sakuramil drug substance does not contain any functional group as nitro-alkyl, oxime, or other functionality that could form N-nitrosamine upon degradation. Therefore, the risk for the formation of nitrosamines due to this root cause is considered as not applicable.

10 Oxidation of hydrazine or other amine-containing functional groups present in active substances or their impurities/degradants (e.g. from hydrazones and hydrazides), either in active substance manufacturing processes or during storage.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

■ N.A.

Justification: Oxidation of hydrazine or other amine-containing functional groups are not present in Sakuramil final drug substance.

11 Use of certain packaging materials.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

■ N.A.

Justification: No certain packaging materials are used.

12 Reaction of amines leaching from quaternary ammonium anion exchange resins (e.g. used for purification steps) with nitrosating agents present in the liquid phase. In addition, disinfection procedures such as e.g. chlorination, chloro-amination and ozonisation can lead to significant N-nitrosamine generation as by-products in case vulnerable amines are present. Given the source of contamination, risk is related to the concentration of the reactive agent(s) and thus, to the volume of water in or used to dilute a particular product. The same risks could be associated with active substances or finished products manufactured using water purified using similar resins.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

■ N.A.

Justification: No quaternary ammonium anion exchange resins are used. No disinfection procedures are applied. Therefore, the risk for the formation of nitrosamines due to this root cause is considered as not applicable.

Risk factors related to GMP aspects

13 Cross-contamination due to different processes being run successively on the same manufacturing line.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

■ N.A.

Justification: There is no risk on cross-contamination with alkylamines, nitrite or nitrosamines due to the use of multipurpose equipment as adequate cleaning procedures according to ICH Q7: Good Manufacturing Practice Guide for Active Pharmaceutical Ingredients are in place. Therefore, the risk for the presence of nitrosamines due to cross-contamination due to the use of multipurpose equipment is considered as not applicable.

14 Carry-over of impurities between process steps due to operator-related errors or insufficiently detailed batch records such as inadequate phase separations during work-up procedures.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

■ N.A.

Justification: This is ensured through internal procedures.

15 Use of contaminated recovered or recycled materials (e.g. solvents, reagents and catalysts) where the recovery is outsourced to third parties who are not aware of the content of the materials they are processing. Recovery processes carried out in non-dedicated equipment should also be considered.

Risk for the presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

□ Yes

□ No

■ N.A.

Justification: Recovered or recycled materials are not used in the manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance; therefore, the formation of N-nitrosamine impurities is not feasible.

Based on the risk evaluation presented above there is a risk for formation/presence of nitroso-CP-6 in Sakuramil drug substance. Therefore, further mitigation is necessary.

RISK OUTCOME

Based on the risk evaluation conducted and mitigation measures, the risk for presence of nitrosamines is evaluated as:

■ no risk identified

☐ risk identified

The risk evaluation indicates that there is a potential presence of N-nitroso-CP-6 impurity in Sakuramil drug substance. However, according to the analytical testing results it is demonstrated that the levels of N-nitrosamine impurity are below 10% of acceptable limit.  Therefore, there is no risk for the presence of N-nitrosamine impurity in Sakuramil drug substance.

Additional information to support the risk assessment by the drug product manufacturer

Nitrosating agents: Nitrosating agents are not likely to be present in the final API.

Vulnerable/nitrosatable substances: Vulnerable amines are present in the final API.

resource.title: Manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance (IROHA-corp.)
resource.description: Four-step synthesis CP-4 -> CP-5 (in situ) -> CP-6 -> CP-7 -> CP-9 (Sakuramil). Typical commercial batch size 350 kg.

action.title: Step 1
action.description: CP-4 is combined with methyl chloroformate, lithium-tert-butoxide, and tetrahydrofuran, then stirred. Layers are settled and separated. Precipitates are filtered, rinsed with tetrahydrofuran and dried to yield CP-5.

action.title: Step 2
action.description: CP-5 is combined with sodium borohydride, magnesium chloride, and methanol, then filtered after the reaction completes. Hydrochloric acid is added to the filtrate, layers are settled and separated. Organic layer is distilled with ethanol, and the mixture is stirred with water. Resulting precipitate is filtered, rinsed and dried to yield CP-6.

valueCodeableConcept.text: CPP #3.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

action.title: Step 3
action.description: CP-6 is combined with tetrahydrofuran, sodium carbonate, and ethyl chloroformate, then heated to reflux. Upon reaction completion, the mixture is filtered and quenched with sodium hydroxide, n-hexane is added, the layers are separated, and the organic layer is distilled with ethanol and stirred with water (CPP #3.1). After filtering and drying it results in CP-7.

action.title: CPP #3.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

extension.valueString: 98-105 L; then 20 to 35% w/w of ethanol

valueCodeableConcept.text: CPP #4.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

action.title: Step 4
action.description: CP-7 and CP-8 are combined in methylene chloride followed by the addition of tetra-n-butylammonium bromide and aqueous sodium hydroxide solution while mixing. Upon reaction completion, methylene chloride and water are added (CPP #4.1); ethanol content is monitored by IPC #1. The mixture is separated, washed, cooled (CPP #4.2, IPC #2) and concentrated with ethanol. After filtering and drying it results in CP-9 (Sakuramil).

action.title: CPP #4.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

3.2.AP Analytical Procedures (Assay/ID) [Assay/Identification][Sakuramil]

3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description

1.1 Principle

High-performance liquid chromatography (USP <621>)

1.2 Reagents

Reference substances: CP-9 standard

Buffer: Approx. 27.2 mg/ml KH2PO4 in water, pH 5.0 adjusted by addition of NaOH solution 2M.

KH2PO4: analytical grade

NaOH solution 2M: 80 mg/ml NaOH in water

Water: Water for injection

Acetonitrile: analytical grade

Diluent: Acetonitrile: Buffer (1:4)

Blank: Take 5 ml of Acetonitrile and dilute to 50 ml with Diluent

1.3 Chromatography

Column: length 250 mm, internal diameter 4.6 mm

Stationary phase: Silica C 18, 3.5 µm, e.g. Nucleosil 250-C 18, 3.5µm

System: isocratic

Mobile Phase: Acetonitrile / Buffer (40:60)

Flow rate: 1.0 mL/min

Oven temperature: 30 ± 1 °C

Sample injection: 10 µl

Detection: UV, 251 nm

Evaluation: Integration of the peaks referring to product; comparison of the retention times of test and reference solution.

1.4 Procedure

Test solution:

Approximately 0.1 mg/ml of sample to be examined in diluent.

Reference solution:

Approximately 0.1 mg/ml of CP-9 standard in diluent.

1.5 System Suitability Test

Theoretical plates: In the chromatogram of five replicate injections of reference solution, the number of theoretical plates is higher than 3200.

Reproducibility: In the chromatogram of reference solution, the relative standard deviation between peak areas of replicate injections (five injections) is not more than 0.73 %.

1.6 Calculation

The content of CP-9 is calculated according to the following formula:

AM =   Peak area value of CP-9 in the test solution

AS =   Peak area value of CP-9 in the reference solution

CS =   Weight of CP-9 (mg) in the reference solution

CM =   Weight of CP-9 (mg) in the test solution

V =     Assay of CP-9 standard, in %

Report the result “as is”.

3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

For determination of assay of Sakuramil an HPLC method was developed and validated by IROHA-corp. The method is validated in terms of specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, intermediate precision, system suitability and stability of the test solutions.

2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary

In the present report, validation results of the assay test (HPLC) as described in DMF section [[2.3.4.AP Analytical Procedures (Assay/ID) [Assay/Identification] [Sakuramil]]] are compiled and evaluated.

For assay determination by HPLC, specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision, intermediate precision, system suitability and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures.

Following acceptance criteria have been defined in a method validation protocol.

Table 2‑1 Acceptance criteria

Validation ParameterAcceptance CriteriaResults

Range· Minimum 60 to 130 % target concentration ·  If acceptance criteria for linearity are fulfilled, range of the method is demonstrated.The method has been validated for a range of 60% to 130% of the concentration examined (0.1 mg/ml of Sakuramil)

Evaluation of the results confirmed that this HPLC method is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameters specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision as well as stability of the solutions could be demonstrated. Furthermore, the required system suitability criteria for theoretical plates and reproducibility fulfill the respective acceptance criteria. Therefore, also accuracy of the method could be confirmed under the actual conditions of use.

3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

For determination of potentially mutagenic impurities of Sakuramil an HPLC method was developed and validated by IROHA-corp. The method is validated in terms of specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy, robustness, system suitability and stability of the test solutions.

2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary

In the present report, validation results of the determination of potentially mutagenic impurities (HPLC) as described in DMF section [[2.3.3.AP Analytical Procedures (Potentially mutagentic Impurities) [Potentially mutagenic Impurities] [Sakuramil]]] are compiled and evaluated.

The method considers the specified impurity from Sakuramil drug substance as well as total impurities. The specified impurity as per DMF section [[2.3.3.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] is CP-6.

The analytical procedure can be stated validated in accordance with ICH Q2(R2) and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

For determination of potentially mutagenic impurities by HPLC, specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), system suitability and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures.

Peak spectrum bunchWith 5 spectraWith 5 spectra

Evaluation of Recorded Spectra:

• Each of these spectra is compared with the average spectrum (n = 5) of the chromatographic peak. Correspondence is expressed via a similarity factor with values between 1000 (identical spectra) and 0 (no match).

• The plot of similarity factors along the chromatographic peak gives the similarity curve.

• A purity factor is calculated taking both the similarity and threshold values into account (values between 1000 and 0).

Calculation of the Peak Purity:

• The mean of all purity values gives the purity factor (= match factor).

• The match factor is calculated for the CP-9 peak as well as for impurity peaks > 0.10 %.

Acceptance Criteria Stability-Indicating Testing / Peak Purity:

• adequate selectivity is given

• observed level > 70.0 % → match factor ≥ 995.0

• observed level > 5.0 % → match factor ≥ 950.0

• observed level > 0.5 % → match factor ≥ 900.0

• observed level > 0.1 % → match factor ≥ 800.0

2.4 Conclusion

Evaluation of the results confirmed that the HPLC method used for determination of related substances in Sakuramil is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameter specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy and robustness as well as stability indicating capability fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.

Robustness of the method with regards to variation of following chromatographic conditions is given:

• column temperature: 23 to 30 °C

• flow rate: 1.1 to 1.3 mL/min

• pH of eluents: 4.8 to 5.0

• variation of column lot

Additionally, the stability of reference solution and test solution stored at RT have been demonstrated. A possible holdup time of at least 28 hours was defined for the reference solution and of maximum of 20 hours for the test solution, respectively.

Furthermore, following response correction factors in relation to Sakuramil (RCFs to be multiplied with) were determined:

CP-6=1.19

3.2.AP.2 Analytical Procedure Validation/Qualification

For determination of related substances of Sakuramil an HPLC method was developed and validated by IROHA-corp. The method is validated in terms of specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy, robustness, system suitability and stability of the test solutions.

2.1 Acceptance Criteria and Summary

In the present report, validation results of the determination of related substances test (HPLC) as described in DMF section [[2.3.3.AP Analytical Procedures (Related Substances)[Purity][Sakuramil]]] are compiled and evaluated.

The method considers all specified impurities from Sakuramil drug substance as well as unspecified impurities. Specified impurities as per DMF section [[2.3.3.DS.C Control (Sakuramil) [IROHA-corp]]] are CP-8 and CP-9-1.

The analytical procedure can be stated validated in accordance with ICH Q2(R2) and used for GxP release analysis of Sakuramil at IROHA-corp.

For determination of related substances by HPLC, specificity, linearity, range, accuracy, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), system suitability and stability of the test solutions were considered as analytical performance characteristics according to current ICH guideline Q2(R2) Validation of Analytical Procedures.

2.3.13.2 Evaluation of Data

Evaluation was carried out by visual examination of chromatograms and purity graphical plot in addition by UV-diode array peak purity.

The impurities (> 0.10 %) as well as the observed degradation level calculated as decrease of the CP-9 peak area normalized to actual sample weight compared to the original sample chromatogram are quantified and reported.

Table 2‑35 Detector settings

Detector parameterDAD Value for:
ImpuritiesSakuramil (diluted 1:10)
Peak Purity Start Wavelengthλ = 210λ = 210
Peak Purity End Wavelengthλ = 400λ = 400
Peak Purity Threshold10%0.10%
Enable background subtractionYesYes
Peak spectrum bunchWith 5 spectraWith 5 spectra

Evaluation of Recorded Spectra:

• Each of these spectra is compared with the average spectrum (n = 5) of the chromatographic peak. Correspondence is expressed via a similarity factor with values between 1000 (identical spectra) and 0 (no match).

• The plot of similarity factors along the chromatographic peak gives the similarity curve.

• A purity factor is calculated taking both the similarity and threshold values into account (values between 1000 and 0).

Calculation of the Peak Purity:

• The mean of all purity values gives the purity factor (= match factor).

• The match factor is calculated for the CP-9 peak as well as for impurity peaks > 0.10 %.

Acceptance Criteria Stability-Indicating Testing / Peak Purity:

• adequate selectivity is given

• observed level > 70.0 % → match factor ≥ 995.0

• observed level > 5.0 % → match factor ≥ 950.0

• observed level > 0.5 % → match factor ≥ 900.0

• observed level > 0.1 % → match factor ≥ 800.0

Forced degradation study results showed that the chromatographic methods for determination of related substances and assay are stability indicating with respect to the described conditions. No relevant increase of related substances was observed when the substance was exposed to light stress (conditions according to ICH Q1B). Thus, the product can be considered photostable. Evaluation of the results confirmed that the HPLC method used for determination of related substances in Sakuramil is suitable for the intended use at IROHA-corp. laboratories. Validation parameter specificity, linearity, precision (repeatability, intermediate precision and system precision), limit of quantification (LOQ), limit of detection (LOD), range, accuracy and robustness as well as stability indicating capability fulfill the respective acceptance criteria.

Robustness of the method with regards to variation of following chromatographic conditions is given:

• column temperature: 23 to 30 °C

• flow rate: 1.1 to 1.3 mL/min

• pH of eluents: 4.8 to 5.0

• variation of column lot

Additionally, the stability of reference solution and test solution stored at RT have been demonstrated. A possible holdup time of at least 28 hours was defined for the reference solution and of maximum of 20 hours for the test solution, respectively.
