3.2.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development

The method was designed to ensure biorelevant in vitro performance and consistent results across manufacturing batches.

1. Solubility and Media Selection

Sakuramil is a white solid with low aqueous solubility at room temperature (0.05 mg/mL in water). Solubility varies significantly with pH:

• pH 1.2 (0.1 N HCl): < 0.1 mg/mL

• pH 4.5 (acetate buffer): 5.0 mg/mL

• pH 6.8 (phosphate buffer): 3.2 mg/mL

• pH 8.0 (0.1 N NaOH): 5.1 mg/mL

These results confirm sink conditions at physiological pH and justify the selection of McIlvaine buffer pH 5.0 as the dissolution medium.

2. Apparatus and Test Conditions

Comparative testing using USP Apparatus I (Basket) and II (Paddle) was performed. Apparatus II (Paddle) at 50 ± 2 rpm provided consistent and reproducible results with minimal variability. Use of sinkers was evaluated and found unnecessary. Filter compatibility was assessed, and a suitable material was selected to ensure sample clarity without adsorbing the drug substance.

The standard volume recommended by the USP for the dissolution testing of immediate release products is 900 mL; therefore, this dissolution volume was selected.

During the development phase, sampling timepoints of 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, and 45 were set to adequately characterize the ascending and plateau phases of the dissolution curves. More than 85% of the drug is released within the duration of the dissolution test.

3. Discriminating ability of the dissolution method

The method’s discriminatory capability was confirmed by testing batches with deliberate formulation, and process variations. The procedure successfully detected differences in dissolution behavior, validating its suitability for stability studies and quality control.

4. Deaeration

Deaeration of the medium was evaluated and found to have no impact on dissolution results under the selected conditions. Therefore, deaeration is not required for routine testing.

5. Target Q Value

In accordance with pharmacopoeial guidance, the target Q value was defined as not less than 80% of the labeled amount dissolved within the specified time frame. This specification was supported by data from the batches used in the clinical trials and confirmed during method validation.

6. Final Method Conditions

The finalized method is based on ultraviolet absorption spectroscopy and follows the principles outlined in Ph. Eur. 2.9.3, USP, and JP 6.10. The test is performed using Apparatus II (Paddle) at 50 ± 2 rpm in 900 mL of McIlvaine buffer (pH 5.0), prepared by dissolving sodium phosphate dibasic dihydrate and citric acid in 800 mL of demineralized water, adjusting pH with HCl or NaOH, and completing the volume to 1 L with distilled water. The dissolution temperature is maintained at 37 ± 0.5 °C.

A minimum of six units are tested, one per vessel, in accordance with the acceptance criteria of Ph. Eur., USP, and JP. UV detection is used to determine the absorbance of the test solutions, with reference solutions prepared at approximately 0.25 mg/mL of Sakuramil. Absorbance values are measured using a suitable spectrophotometer, and comparative evaluation is performed when applicable.

7. Conclusion

The dissolution method developed for

Sakura Bloom 20 mg

is scientifically justified, robust, and compliant with international pharmacopoeial standards. It demonstrates reproducibility, discriminatory power, and suitability for routine quality control, comparative dissolution studies, and regulatory submissions. The incorporation of UV detection and McIlvaine buffer at pH 5.0 ensures reliable performance and sensitivity across batches, supporting product quality throughout its shelf life.

3.2.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Description

Dissolution under RTRT is controlled in three-dimensional design space so that the dissolution is about 90% (feedback control of spray rate by FBRM, compression force control by compression force controller).

1) Particle size of drug substance affecting dissolution is a specification item for drug substance which is performed by Laser diffraction particle size distribution analyzer.

2) Granule particle size is monitored using Focused Beam Reflectance Measurement (FBRM).

3) Uncoated tablet hardness is controlled by tablet hardness tester.

The particle size of drug substance is measured as a specification testing in the process of drug substance, by a laser diffraction-scattering type particle size distribution measuring device. Without preparing samples for measurement, the powder of drug substance is measured for particle distribution by the dry method (specification testing of drug substance). Regarding the particle size of the granulation, the particle size at the end of granulation, which is obtained by a FBRM method is used. The uncoated tablet hardness is measured in 200 tablets (10 tablets × 20 time points) sampled over time.

Dissolution test was performed for the drug product manufactured under the conditions allocated by DoE, and the affect of each factor on the dissolution rate were investigated. The test results were subjected to multidimensional analysis. For the formula for the sum of each factor which is multiplied by a coefficient, the coefficients that make the residual sum of squares minimum were calculated (the formula is shown below).

The dissolution rate calculated by the dissolution model at the time point of 30 minutes is 80% or higher.

By controlling each process using this system, dissolution of the drug product is considered to be assured.

3.2.AP.3 Analytical Procedure Development

1. Objective

To develop a Real-Time Release Testing (RTRT) method for monitoring and predicting the dissolution behavior of pharmaceutical solid dosage forms using ultraviolet (UV) spectroscopy.

---

2. Principle

UV spectroscopy measures the absorbance of UV light by a drug substance in solution. The absorbance at specific wavelengths correlates with the concentration of the dissolved active pharmaceutical ingredient (API), enabling real-time monitoring of dissolution.

---

3. Critical Quality Attributes (CQAs)

• Primary CQA: Dissolution rate

• Supporting CQAs:

• API concentration in solution

• Absorbance at characteristic UV wavelengths

• pH and temperature of dissolution medium

---

4. Process Analytical Technology (PAT) Tools
PAT ToolPurpose
UV SpectrophotometerReal-time monitoring of API concentration in dissolution medium
pH and Temperature ProbesControl and monitor dissolution conditions
Flow-through Cell or Fiber Optic ProbeIn-situ sampling and measurement

---

5. Predictive Modeling Approach

• Model Type: Calibration curve or multivariate regression (e.g., PLS)

• Input Variables: Absorbance values at selected wavelengths, time, pH, temperature

• Output Variable: Dissolution profile (concentration vs. time)

• Model Basis: Beer-Lambert Law:

A=ε⋅c⋅lA=ε⋅c⋅l

where:

• AA: absorbance

• εε: molar absorptivity

• cc: concentration

• ll: path length

---

6. Method Development Steps

• Wavelength Selection: Identify optimal wavelength(s) for API detection.

• Calibration Curve: Prepare standard solutions and generate absorbance vs. concentration curve.

• Dissolution Testing: Conduct dissolution studies with in-line UV monitoring.

• Model Building: Correlate real-time absorbance data with dissolution profiles.

• Validation: Validate the method per ICH Q2(R2) for accuracy, precision, linearity, and robustness.

• Implementation: Integrate UV probe into dissolution apparatus for RTRT.

---

7. Regulatory Considerations

• Follow USP <711> for dissolution testing and USP <857> for UV-Vis spectroscopy.

• Ensure proper calibration and maintenance of UV equipment.

• Validate the method for specificity, especially in the presence of excipients or degradation products.

2.3.4. AP Analytical Procedures (MET)[Purity][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]

2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification

The requirements are set in accordance with the harmonised monographs of Ph. Eur. 5.1.4 ‘Microbiological quality of non-sterile pharmaceutical preparations and substances for pharmaceutical use’, USP <1111> ‘Microbiological examination of nonsterile products: acceptance criteria for pharmaceutical preparations and substances for pharmaceutical use’ and JP <G4> ‘Microbial Attributes of Non-sterile Pharmaceutical Products’.

Total aerobic microbial count (TAMC) and total combined yeasts/ moulds count (TYMC) are assessed by the plate count method in accordance with the harmonized method Ph. Eur. 2.6.12 “Microbiological examination of Non-Sterile Products: Microbial Enumeration Tests”, USP <61>: “Microbiological examination of Nonsterile Products: Microbial Enumeration Tests” and JP <4.05> “1. Microbiological Examination of Non-Sterile Products: Microbial Enumeration Tests”.

The absence of specific microorganism Escherichia coli is assessed according to Ph. Eur. 2.6.13 “Harmonized Method: Microbiological Examination of Non-Sterile Products: Tests for Specified Micro-Organisms”, USP <62> “Microbiological Examination of Non-sterile Products: Tests for Specified Microorganisms” and JP <4.05> “2. Microbiological Examination of Non-Sterile Products: Tests for Specified Micro-Organisms”.

MET is proposed to be performed as a frequency test (periodic quality indicator test). The risk of microbial contamination of the drug product is considered low due to the manufacturing process, environmental monitoring, and cleaning procedures in place. The entire process is a dry granulation, blending and compression, and does not use any water or other microbial-growth supporting solvents, except during the coating step.

Water activity results of less than 0.2 for the final blend, uncoated and coated tablets (Table 1 and Table 2), as well as the historical MET data supports this assessment (Table 3 and Table 4). During development, microbial enumeration testing was performed on 3 pilot-scale/registration stability batches (i.e., ABC123, ABC456 and ABC789). For all batches tested to date, the results met the proposed requirements. Furthermore, no microbial growth was observed at 6-month registration stability testing point in either blister packaging under accelerated conditions (Table 4).

Therefore, the proposal to perform MET as frequency test is consistent with the ICH guideline Q6A (Decision tree #8). The microbial enumeration tests will be performed at release on the first 5 consecutive production batches. If the requirements are met, testing frequency may be reduced to every 10th batch. At least one batch will be tested in each calendar year in which the product is manufactured.

2.3.4. AP Analytical Procedures (Dissolution/UV)[Performance][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]

2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification

Dissolution testing is performed in accordance with the Ph. Eur. 2.9.3 “Dissolution test for solid dosage forms”, Acceptance Table 1 of USP <711> “Dissolution”, or JP <6.10> “Dissolution test” (harmonized method), using the paddle method (apparatus 2) at 50 ± 2 rpm and 900 mL of 4.0 N McIlvaine buffer as the dissolution medium. The USP apparatus 2 (paddle) method was chosen based on the dosage form.

Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is an immediate release product. The speed of 50 rpm is considered standard for the paddle apparatus to provide agitation for an immediate release product. The setting of Q-value and Q-time is based on the release and stability data obtained for batch ABC123 used in registration stability. It was established to ensure that sufficient in vitro release can be achieved. No other batches of Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablet were used in clinical trials in support of this marketing authorization application. Nevertheless, the requirements previously mentioned are also supported by the dissolution data obtained for the registration stability batches ABC123 and ABC456. The specifications follow the Acceptance Table 1 of USP <711> “Dissolution”, Ph. Eur. 2.9.3 “Dissolution test for solid dosage forms”, JP <6.10> “Dissolution test” (harmonized method) for S1 and S2 testing for release and for stages 1, 2 and 3 for stability. This test is performed at release and during stability.

A detailed discussion on the choice of the dissolution method as well as dissolution profile data for these batches are provided in [[2.1 Dissolution testing]].

Medium deaeration was evaluated and showed no impact on dissolution. Batches with original formulation, medium with deliberate formulation (e.g. (such as higher magnesium stearate) and process variation (such as larger API particle size) were tested, showing distinct dissolution behaviors under different conditions. The finalized dissolution method for Sakura Bloom 20 mg as depicted in [[2.3.3. AP Analytical Procedures (Dissolution/UV)[Performance][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]]] is scientifically justified, robust, and compliant with international pharmacopoeial standards. It demonstrates reproducibility, discriminatory power, and suitability for routine quality control, comparative dissolution studies, and regulatory submissions. The incorporation of UV detection and McIlvaine buffer at pH 5.0 ensures reliable performance and sensitivity across batches, supporting product quality throughout its shelf life.

2.3.4. AP Analytical Procedures (Dissolution/RTRT)[Performance][Sakura Bloom 20 mg]

2.3.4.AP.1 Analytical Procedure Justification

A feedforward control will be performed as an operation in commercial production so that the dissolution rate is about 90%. In other words, a control to keep the predicted dissolution value being always constant will be made by appropriately determining the target value for a granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness within this design space according to the particle size of drug substance.

The particle size of drug substance is measured as a specification testing in the process of drug substance, by a laser diffraction-scattering type particle size distribution measuring device. Without preparing samples for measurement, the powder of drug substance is measured for particle distribution by the dry method (specification testing of drug substance). Regarding the particle size of the granulation, the particle size at the end of granulation, which is obtained by a FBRM method is used. The uncoated tablet hardness is measured in 200 tablets (10 tablets over 20 time points) sampled over time.

The integration of UV spectroscopy with appropriate calibration models and process controls ensures consistent product quality and supports continuous manufacturing initiatives. This RTRT strategy aligns with regulatory expectations for Process Analytical Technology (PAT) and Quality by Design (QbD), offering enhanced process understanding, faster batch release, and improved operational efficiency.

1 Introduction

The HPLC method for the identification of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets was validated according to the method validation protocol VP_SB_21_2021.  Test method for identity by HPLC, employs the identical chromatographic conditions stipulated in Analytical procedure document. Hence, the validation of identification method was performed simultaneously with the validation of the assay and related substances method.

This document reports the validation results which show that the method is suitable for the identification of Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil in Sakura Bloom Film-coated tablets.  The method has been shown to be specific for the identification of Sakura Bloom Film-coated tablets.

2 Reference standard and materials

The reference standard and materials used in the validation of test method are described in Analytical procedure document.

3 Results and discussion

Identification by HPLC was evaluated by preparing and injecting blank, placebo, reference standard and placebo spiked with Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil at 100% level (20 mg strength) solutions into an HPLC system according to assay/related substances method.  A validation protocol, VP_SB_21_2021 was prepared for the identification method, the necessary validation data are extracted from validation report of assay and related substances method, VR_SB_21_2021 addendum as these two methods are identical.

Representative chromatograms of blank (diluent and extraction solvent), placebo solution, reference standard and spiked placebo solution with Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil at 100% level (20 mg strength) are illustrated in Figure 4-1 and Figure 4-2.  These chromatograms indicate that there is no interference from the blank and placebo injections with the Sakura Bloom and Sakuramil peaks.  Therefore, the test method identity by HPLC, is suitable for its intended use.

Risk evaluation of Nitrosamine impurities in Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet

The risk evaluation for the potential presence of Nitrosamine impurities, belonging to the mutagenic impurity cohort of concern (CoC) according to the ICH M7 guideline, has been performed.

The risk evaluation for Nitrosamine impurities follows the guidelines indicated below and is also

aligned with the requirements of further National Competent Authorities globally:

• Assessment report Article 5(3) of Regulation EC (No) 726/2004 ‘Nitrosamine impurities

in human medicinal products’ (EMA/369136/2020) and ‘Questions and answers for

marketing authorization holders/applicants on the CHMP Opinion for the Article 5(3) of

Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 referral on nitrosamine impurities in human medicinal

products’ (EMA/409815/2020, current revision).

• FDA Control of Nitrosamine Impurities in Human Drugs, Guidance for Industry, current

version

The contribution of the following factors to the potential presence of Nitrosamine impurities in

medicinal product are evaluated regarding:

The materials and their quality:

• Drug substance

• Drug product manufacturing process;

• excipients;

• primary packaging material(s).

Drug substance

The risk evaluation for the potential presence of Nitrosamine impurities due to the drug substance

(DS) process is documented in the drug substance risk evaluation [[2.1.2 Nitrosamine impurities]]

CP-6, which contains a secondary amine moiety, is included in the final API specification with a limit of NMT 37.5 ppm.

Excipients

The excipients used in the drug product were evaluated for their potential contribution to the

presence / formation of Nitrosamine impurities in the drug product. Table 2 below assesses the

excipients based on their structure and the potential contribution that they can have on formation

of N-nitroso compounds in the drug product.

Table 2 : Drug Product Excipients and Potential Contribution to Nitrosamine impurities presence / formation in the Drug Product Manufacturing Process

DescriptionExcipient
Excipients that neither have a structural alert for the presence or formation of N-nitrosamines, nor have risk for presence of vulnerable amines, but for which the presence of the nitrosating agent nitrite cannot be excluded. Based on available data on nitrite levels in excipients, the levels of reactive impurities such as nitrite are generally expected to be less than 10 ppm. These excipients can contribute to the risk of N-nitrosamine formation. These excipients have to be considered, in cases the API is reactive to trace amounts of nitrite and the nitrosation reaction is possible under the DP process conditions.Lactose monohydrate Microcrystalline cellulose Croscarmellose sodium Hydroxypropyl cellulose Magnesium stearate
Excipients that do not have a structural alert for the presence or formation of N-nitrosamines.Coating premix red

Drug Product Manufacturing Process

No nitrosating reagents are used in the process on drug

product equipment at the manufacturing site facility. No recycled or recovered materials are

used. The drug product equipment is not passivated with nitric acid or cleaned with chlorine or

chloramine. There are no nitrosating agents or nitrosamines that could be in contact with the

product during the manufacturing process.

There is a theoretical potential risk of nitrosamine impurity formation in the wet

granulation/drying process, where the API is initially suspended in water and afterwards the

wet granulated mass is dried by heating. Nonetheless, heat introduced during the drying phase

drives water evaporation, and the process is controlled to stop drying upon achievement of loss

on drying (LOD) limit.

Although CP-6 is controlled in the drug substance at tight limit of 37.5 ppm, during drug product manufacturing in presence of nitrosating agent precursors (e.g. nitrites from the excipients) there exists a potential theoretical risk for conversion to the respective Nitrosamine impurity N-Nitroso-CP-6 . Testing performed on three recent representative, production-scale and commercial batches (including samples of three batches stored under accelerated stability conditions) applying a quantification limit down to 10% of the acceptable intake (AI) limit however confirmed the absence.

Primary packaging material(s).

The current drug product primary packaging material consists of a HDPE bottle with desiccant

with polypropylene (PP) child resistant closure cap (or) PA/AL/PVC blister. There is no risk of Nitrosamine impurities formation / contamination of the drug product from the primary packaging material and process. There is also no risk from interaction of the solid dosage form with the primary packaging.

Risk of Increase/Formation of N-nitroso compounds during Storage

Based on 6 months accelerated stability at 40°C/75% RH available for 6 batches, there is no risk of increase/formation of Nitrosamine impurities during stability

Based on this evaluation, there is no risk for the presence of N-nitroso compounds (N-Nitroso-CP-6) in Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablet. PAT (Process analytical technology) - RTRT strategy justification

This document provides a scientific and regulatory justification for the implementation of Real-Time Release Testing (RTRT) for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet. The proposed RTRT strategy complements end-product testing with in-process controls and predictive models, ensuring consistent product quality and compliance with regulatory expectations.

---

1. RTRT Scope and Strategy

---

RTRT will be applied to the following critical quality attributes (CQAs). The other CQA remains subject to conventional end-product testing.

CQARTRT MethodologyTraditional Method Replaced
IdentificationNIR spectroscopy during compressionHPLC
Content UniformityNIR spectroscopy during blendingUniformity of dosage units
DissolutionPredictive model based on process dataUSP dissolution test

In case of RTRT unavailability or model failure, conventional methods will be applied as a fallback approach.

---

2. Scientific Justification
2.1 Process Understanding

Extensive development studies have established a robust design space for blending, granulation, and compression. Critical process parameters (CPPs) are tightly controlled and correlated with CQAs. Risk assessments (ICH Q9) confirm confirm that the RTRT approach is commensurate with the level of process knowledge established during development.

2.2 Analytical Technology

• NIR Spectroscopy: Validated for quantitative assay and uniformity.

• Compression Force Sensors: Provide real-time feedback on tablet hardness and weight.

• Multivariate Models: Chemometric models predict dissolution profiles with high accuracy.

Calibration, maintenance, and data integrity measures are implemented to ensure robustness of PAT tools and multivariate models.

2.3 Validation

• RTRT methods have been validated against conventional release tests.

• Comparative studies demonstrate equivalence or superiority in detecting out-of-specification conditions.

• Model lifecycle management includes periodic revalidation and performance monitoring.

Cross-reference: Details on the development of RTRT methods are presented in section [[(Sakura bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg] ]]

3. Lifecycle management and Change control

RTRT models and PAT tools are managed under the Pharmaceutical Quality System (ICH Q10). Ongoing lifecycle activities include continuous monitoring, periodic review, and predefined acceptance criteria for recalibration. All updates are subject to formal change control, with regulatory reporting where applicable.

action.description: NMT 2                                      RSD of Sakuramil peak in replicate injections of standard solution should not be more than 0.75 %

action.title: Identification
action.description: Assess the peak for Sakuramil in the chromatogram of test solution 1 and assess the peak for Sakuramil in the reference solution with respect to retention time. The difference should not exceed ± 2.0 %.

action.title: Assay

action.title: Degradation products related to Sakuramil
action.description: Determine the peak area for CP-9-1 and any further unspecified degradation products individually in the chromatogram of test solution 1 and the peak area for Sakuramil in the chromatogram of the reference solution. Disregard any peaks < 0.1 %.

action.title: CP-9-1
action.description: Determine the peak area for CP-9-1 in the chromatogram of test solution 2 and the peak area for Sakuramil in the chromatogram of the reference solution. Disregard any other peaks and CP-9-1 peaks < 0.01 %. Percent content of total degradation products, based on the declared content of Sakuramil. Total all values obtained for the individual degradation products.

action.title: Step 1 - Pre-blending
action.description: Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance in a diffusion mixer (bin blender).

action.title: Step 2 - Preparation of granulation liquid
action.description: Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

action.title: Step 3 - Granulation
action.description: Load the pre-blended material into a fluid bed granulator and add the granulation liquid to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules.

action.title: Step 4 - Drying
action.description: Dry the granules using the dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit until loss on drying of 1 - 2 % is achieved.

action.title: Step 5 - Screening
action.description: Sieve the dried granules using a screening mill.

action.title: Step 6 - Lubricant addition
action.description: Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen and add it to the granules.

action.title: Step 7 - Final blending
action.description: Blend the mixture using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

action.title: Step 8 - Tablet compression
action.description: Compress the final blend using a tablet press to obtain the tablet cores.

action.title: Step 9 - Preparation of the coating suspension
action.description: Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water.

action.title: Step 10 - Film-coating
action.description: Film-coat the tablet cores using the film-coat suspension in a coating pan to achieve the desired film-coat weight gain, followed by drying.

action.title: Step 11 - Inspection
action.description: Collect 10 tablets to perform the Description test and Identification test (RTRT).

action.title: Step 12 - Primary packaging
action.description: The film-coated tablets are primary packaged (HDPE bottle or PA/AL/PVC blister).

action.title: Step 13 - Secondary packaging
action.description: The primary packaged product is packed in a cardboard-based secondary pack.

resource.description: Four-step synthesis CP-4 -> CP-5 (in situ) -> CP-6 -> CP-7 -> CP-9 (Sakuramil). Typical commercial batch size 350 kg.

action.title: Step 1
action.description: CP-4 is combined with methyl chloroformate, lithium-tert-butoxide, and tetrahydrofuran, then stirred. Layers are settled and separated. Precipitates are filtered, rinsed with tetrahydrofuran and dried to yield CP-5.

action.title: Step 2
action.description: CP-5 is combined with sodium borohydride, magnesium chloride, and methanol, then filtered after the reaction completes. Hydrochloric acid is added to the filtrate, layers are settled and separated. Organic layer is distilled with ethanol, and the mixture is stirred with water. Resulting precipitate is filtered, rinsed and dried to yield CP-6.

valueCodeableConcept.text: CPP #3.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

action.title: Step 3
action.description: CP-6 is combined with tetrahydrofuran, sodium carbonate, and ethyl chloroformate, then heated to reflux. Upon reaction completion, the mixture is filtered and quenched with sodium hydroxide, n-hexane is added, the layers are separated, and the organic layer is distilled with ethanol and stirred with water (CPP #3.1). After filtering and drying it results in CP-7.

action.title: CPP #3.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

extension.valueString: 98-105 L; then 20 to 35% w/w of ethanol

valueCodeableConcept.text: CPP #4.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

action.title: Step 4
action.description: CP-7 and CP-8 are combined in methylene chloride followed by the addition of tetra-n-butylammonium bromide and aqueous sodium hydroxide solution while mixing. Upon reaction completion, methylene chloride and water are added (CPP #4.1); ethanol content is monitored by IPC #1. The mixture is separated, washed, cooled (CPP #4.2, IPC #2) and concentrated with ethanol. After filtering and drying it results in CP-9 (Sakuramil).

action.title: CPP #4.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

action.title: Step 1 - Pre-blending
action.description: Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance in a diffusion mixer (bin blender).

action.title: Step 2 - Preparation of granulation liquid
action.description: Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

action.title: Step 3 - Granulation
action.description: Load the pre-blended material into a fluid bed granulator and add the granulation liquid to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules.

action.title: Step 4 - Drying
action.description: Dry the granules using the dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit until loss on drying of 1 - 2 % is achieved.

action.title: Step 5 - Screening
action.description: Sieve the dried granules using a screening mill.

action.title: Step 6 - Lubricant addition
action.description: Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen and add it to the granules.

action.title: Step 7 - Final blending
action.description: Blend the mixture using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

action.title: Step 8 - Tablet compression
action.description: Compress the final blend using a tablet press to obtain the tablet cores.

action.title: Step 9 - Preparation of the coating suspension
action.description: Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water.

action.title: Step 10 - Film-coating
action.description: Film-coat the tablet cores using the film-coat suspension in a coating pan to achieve the desired film-coat weight gain, followed by drying.

action.title: Step 11 - Inspection
action.description: Collect 10 tablets to perform the Description test and Identification test (RTRT).

action.title: Step 12 - Primary packaging
action.description: The film-coated tablets are primary packaged (HDPE bottle or PA/AL/PVC blister).

action.title: Step 13 - Secondary packaging
action.description: The primary packaged product is packed in a cardboard-based secondary pack.

Start of shelf life

The calculation of the expiration period of a batch complies with the requirements as stated in the EU guideline NfG on Start of Shelf-Life of the Finished Dosage Form (CPMP/QWP/ 072/96).

The following approach is taken in practice:

The expiration period of a production batch is calculated from the date of production of that batch. The date of production of a batch is no later than the step in the manufacturing process where the active ingredient is combined with other ingredients.

action.title: Step 1 - Pre-blending
action.description: Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance in a diffusion mixer (bin blender).

action.title: Step 2 - Preparation of granulation liquid
action.description: Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

action.title: Step 3 - Granulation
action.description: Load the pre-blended material into a fluid bed granulator and add the granulation liquid to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules.

action.title: Step 4 - Drying
action.description: Dry the granules using the dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit until loss on drying of 1 - 2 % is achieved.

action.title: Step 5 - Screening
action.description: Sieve the dried granules using a screening mill.

action.title: Step 6 - Lubricant addition
action.description: Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen and add it to the granules.

action.title: Step 7 - Final blending
action.description: Blend the mixture using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

action.title: Step 8 - Tablet compression
action.description: Compress the final blend using a tablet press to obtain the tablet cores.

action.title: Step 9 - Preparation of the coating suspension
action.description: Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water.

action.title: Step 10 - Film-coating
action.description: Film-coat the tablet cores using the film-coat suspension in a coating pan to achieve the desired film-coat weight gain, followed by drying.

action.title: Step 11 - Inspection
action.description: Collect 10 tablets to perform the Description test and Identification test (RTRT).

action.title: Step 12 - Primary packaging
action.description: The film-coated tablets are primary packaged (HDPE bottle or PA/AL/PVC blister).

action.title: Step 13 - Secondary packaging
action.description: The primary packaged product is packed in a cardboard-based secondary pack.

2.3.4.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom )[APM][FCT][20 mg]

2.3.4.DP.S.1 Container closure system

The bulk Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets are packaged in a primary container consisting of a PETP/AL/PE aluminum composite bag, which is tightly sealed to provide an adequate moisture and oxygen barrier. It has demonstrated its suitability for maintaining the chemical and physical stability of the bulk product under the proposed storage conditions.

The batch analysis results are provided in [[3.2.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

2.3.4.DP.S.2 Stability, storage conditions, and shelf life

The stability data generated for Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets stored in PETP/AL/PE composite bags demonstrate that the bulk product remains chemically and physically stable for up to 18 months under long-term storage conditions (25°C/60% RH and 30°C/75% RH). Across both production batches (ABC123 and ABC456), the following results were observed: assay values ranging from 97.4% to 100.9%, total degradation products ranging from 0.2% to 0.4%, unspecified degradation products were consistently reported as <0.2%, and appearance remained unchanged throughout the study period under both conditions. Dissolution after 30 minutes ranged from 92% to 101% (25 °C/60% RH) and 92% to 100% (30 °C/75% RH), meeting the dissolution specification and showing no significant trend. Stability under accelerated conditions (40°C/75% RH) for up to 6 months further supports the stability of the product. Based on these data, a holding time of 18 months is proposed for the bulk product when stored at or below 30°C in tightly sealed PETP/AL/PE bags. These conditions also support intermediate storage and transport under excursions up to 40°C for a limited duration.

The supportive stability study reports for bulk product are provided in [[3.2.DP.S Storage - Bulk (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

2.3.4.DP.S Storage - Blister (Sakura Bloom )[APM][FCT][20 mg]

2.3.4.DP.S.1 Container closure system

1 Primary packaging materials

Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet for primary stability studies were packaged in the following packaging type commonly used for solid oral dosage forms and found to be suitably stable.

• PA/AL/PVC blister packs, consisting of a polyamide aluminum and polyvinyl chloride film backed with a heat sealable lacquered aluminum foil.

During development of the tablets, different primary packaging types have been considered and tested. On the basis of the stability data generated during development and registration batches, PA/AL/PVC blisters and HDPE bottles with induction sealing and child-resistant cap were selected as primary packaging of first choice. These container types possess favorable properties resulting in sufficient quality characteristics of tablets during the shelf-life. Suitability of these container closure systems is well established by stability data of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets.

Microbiological attributes

Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is a standard solid oral dosage form. Controls necessary for the manufacture and control of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet are conducted in accordance with cGMPs to prevent microbial contamination.

However, routine microbiological testing is unnecessary as the drug product has no propensity to support microbial growth. Hence, Microbiological Enumeration Testing (MET) is performed as a periodic/skip testing. The control strategy for microbiological attributes is described in [[2.3.4.DP.C Control (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

The detailed information on primary packaging materials selected for commercial supplies, is provided in [[2.3.3.DP.S Storage - Blister (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg] ]]

2.3.4.DP.S.2 Stability, storage conditions, and shelf life

Three primary stability batches and three commitment stability batches have been manufactured at the commercial scale. The primary were manufactured with the commercial manufacturing process described in [[2.3.3.DP.M Manufacture - Core section (Sakura Bloom)[APM[FCT][20 mg]]]. The primary stability lots are manufactured with the tablet formulation presented in [[2.3.3.DP.D Description (Sakura Bloom)[APARNA-pharm][FCT][20 mg]]] and are packaged in the commercial container closure system as described in [[2.3.3.DP.S.1 Container Closure System]].

1 Stability Summary and Conclusions

The stability program for Batches 123, 456, and 789 was designed to comprehensively evaluate the product's performance under various environmental conditions to support its registration and commercialization. The study encompassed long-term stability assessments at 25°C/60% RH and 30°C/75% RH over a 36-month period, accelerated stability testing at 40°C/75% RH for up to 6 months, and photostability evaluations to determine sensitivity to light exposure. All data were collected using validated analytical methods and monitored for critical quality attributes such as assay, impurities, dissolution and physical appearance.

1. Assay (% Label Claim)

Across all conditions (25°C/60% RH, 30°C/75% RH, 40°C/75% RH), assay values remain within a tight range: 98.1% to 101.4%. Slight upward trend at 40°C/75% RH, especially in batch ABC789 (up to 101.4%).

While some variability in assay data was reported no stability trend was observed.

Assay remains well within acceptable limits across all conditions. No significant degradation or potency loss observed, even under accelerated conditions.

---

2. Degradation Products (%)

CP-9-1:

Results consistently < 0.10% across all conditions and batches. Occasional detection at 0.10%, but still within specification.

Individual Unspecified Impurities:

• Mostly Not Detected (ND) or < 0.10%.

Total Impurities:

• Slight increase with temperature:

• 25°C/60% RH: up to 0.11%

• 30°C/75% RH: up to 0.14%

• 40°C/75% RH: up to 0.17%

Impurity levels are low and stable. Slight increase in total impurities at higher temperatures is expected and within acceptable limits.

---

3. Dissolution (% in 30 minutes)

All batches show dissolution between 94% to 106%. Slight increase in dissolution at 40°C/75% RH, possibly due to enhanced solubility.

Dissolution performance is robust across all conditions. No adverse impact from storage conditions.

---

Parameters such as appearance remained unchanged through the shelf-life

Based on the available drug product stability data provided in [[3.2.DP.S Storage - Blister (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]] , the proposed packaging is considered protective and compatible with Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet and was stable for not less than 36 months. 2.3.4.DP.S Storage - Bottle (Sakura Bloom )[APM][FCT][20 mg]

2.3.4.DP.S.1 Container closure system

1 Primary packaging materials

Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet for primary stability studies were packaged in the following packaging type commonly used for solid oral dosage forms and found to be suitably stable.

• Standard high density polyethylene (HDPE) bottles with child resistant closure and aluminum induction seal.

During development of the tablets, different primary packaging types have been considered and tested. On the basis of the stability data generated during development and registration batches, PA/AL/PVC blisters and HDPE bottles with induction sealing and child-resistant cap were selected as primary packaging of first choice. These container types possess favorable properties to guarantee the quality characteristics of tablets during the shelf-life. Suitability of these container closure systems is well established by stability data of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablets.

Microbiological attributes

Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet is a standard solid oral dosage form. Controls necessary for the manufacture and control of Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet are conducted in accordance with cGMPs to prevent microbial contamination.

However, routine microbiological testing is unnecessary as the drug product has no propensity to support microbial growth. Hence, Microbiological Enumeration Testing (MET) is performed as a periodic/skip testing. The control strategy for microbiological attributes is described in [[2.3.4.DP.C Control (Sakura Bloom)[APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

The stability data for these studies are provided in Section [[3.2.DP.S Storage - Bottle (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]].

1 Stability Summary and conclusions

The stability program for Batches 123, 456, and 789 was designed to comprehensively evaluate the product's performance under various environmental conditions to support its registration and commercialization. The study encompassed long-term stability assessments at 25°C/60% RH and 30°C/75% RH over a 36-month period, accelerated stability testing at 40°C/75% RH for up to 6 months, and photostability evaluations to determine sensitivity to light exposure. All data were collected using validated analytical methods and monitored for critical quality attributes such as assay, impurities, dissolution and physical appearance.

1. Assay (% Label Claim)

Across all conditions (25°C/60% RH, 30°C/75% RH, 40°C/75% RH), assay values remain within a tight range: 98.1% to 101.4%. Slight upward trend at 40°C/75% RH, especially in batch ABC789 (up to 101.4%).

While some variability in assay data was reported no stability trend was observed.

Assay remains well within acceptable limits across all conditions. No significant degradation or potency loss observed, even under accelerated conditions.

---

2. Degradation Products (%)

CP-9-1:

Results consistently < 0.10% across all conditions and batches. Occasional detection at 0.10%, but still within specification.

Individual Unspecified Impurities:

• Mostly Not Detected (ND) or < 0.10%.

Total Impurities:

• Slight increase with temperature:

• 25°C/60% RH: up to 0.11%

• 30°C/75% RH: up to 0.14%

• 40°C/75% RH: up to 0.17%

Impurity levels are low and stable. Slight increase in total impurities at higher temperatures is expected and within acceptable limits.

---

3. Dissolution (% in 30 minutes)

All batches show dissolution between 94% to 106%. Slight increase in dissolution at 40°C/75% RH, possibly due to enhanced solubility.

Dissolution performance is robust across all conditions. No adverse impact from storage conditions.

---

Parameters such as appearance remained unchanged through the shelf-life

Based on the available drug product stability data provided in [[3.2.DP.S Storage - Bottle (Sakura Bloom) [APM][FCT][20 mg]]] , the proposed packaging is considered protective and compatible with Sakura Bloom 20 mg Film-coated tablet and was stable for not less than 36 months. text.div: PlanDefinition Wet (fluid-bed) granulation, blending, compression and film-coating. Commercial batch size 520.00 kg (approx. 2,600,000 tablets). No overages. Critical steps: granulation (step 3) and compression (step 8); granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness are controlled within a design space to ensure dissolution.

resource.title: Manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablets (Aparna Pharmaceutical Manufacturing)
resource.description: Wet (fluid-bed) granulation, blending, compression and film-coating. Commercial batch size 520.00 kg (approx. 2,600,000 tablets). No overages. Critical steps: granulation (step 3) and compression (step 8); granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness are controlled within a design space to ensure dissolution.

action.title: Step 1 - Pre-blending
action.description: Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance in a diffusion mixer (bin blender).

action.title: Step 2 - Preparation of granulation liquid
action.description: Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

action.title: Step 3 - Granulation
action.description: Load the pre-blended material into a fluid bed granulator and add the granulation liquid to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules.

action.title: Step 4 - Drying
action.description: Dry the granules using the dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit until loss on drying of 1 - 2 % is achieved.

action.title: Step 5 - Screening
action.description: Sieve the dried granules using a screening mill.

action.title: Step 6 - Lubricant addition
action.description: Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen and add it to the granules.

action.title: Step 7 - Final blending
action.description: Blend the mixture using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

action.title: Step 8 - Tablet compression
action.description: Compress the final blend using a tablet press to obtain the tablet cores.

action.title: Step 9 - Preparation of the coating suspension
action.description: Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water.

action.title: Step 10 - Film-coating
action.description: Film-coat the tablet cores using the film-coat suspension in a coating pan to achieve the desired film-coat weight gain, followed by drying.

action.title: Step 11 - Inspection
action.description: Collect 10 tablets to perform the Description test and Identification test (RTRT).

action.title: Step 12 - Primary packaging
action.description: The film-coated tablets are primary packaged (HDPE bottle or PA/AL/PVC blister).

action.title: Step 13 - Secondary packaging
action.description: The primary packaged product is packed in a cardboard-based secondary pack.

resource.title: Manufacturing process of Sakuramil drug substance (IROHA-corp.)
resource.description: Four-step synthesis CP-4 -> CP-5 (in situ) -> CP-6 -> CP-7 -> CP-9 (Sakuramil). Typical commercial batch size 350 kg.

action.title: Step 1
action.description: CP-4 is combined with methyl chloroformate, lithium-tert-butoxide, and tetrahydrofuran, then stirred. Layers are settled and separated. Precipitates are filtered, rinsed with tetrahydrofuran and dried to yield CP-5.

action.title: Step 2
action.description: CP-5 is combined with sodium borohydride, magnesium chloride, and methanol, then filtered after the reaction completes. Hydrochloric acid is added to the filtrate, layers are settled and separated. Organic layer is distilled with ethanol, and the mixture is stirred with water. Resulting precipitate is filtered, rinsed and dried to yield CP-6.

valueCodeableConcept.text: CPP #3.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

action.title: Step 3
action.description: CP-6 is combined with tetrahydrofuran, sodium carbonate, and ethyl chloroformate, then heated to reflux. Upon reaction completion, the mixture is filtered and quenched with sodium hydroxide, n-hexane is added, the layers are separated, and the organic layer is distilled with ethanol and stirred with water (CPP #3.1). After filtering and drying it results in CP-7.

action.title: CPP #3.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

extension.valueString: 98-105 L; then 20 to 35% w/w of ethanol

valueCodeableConcept.text: CPP #4.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

action.title: Step 4
action.description: CP-7 and CP-8 are combined in methylene chloride followed by the addition of tetra-n-butylammonium bromide and aqueous sodium hydroxide solution while mixing. Upon reaction completion, methylene chloride and water are added (CPP #4.1); ethanol content is monitored by IPC #1. The mixture is separated, washed, cooled (CPP #4.2, IPC #2) and concentrated with ethanol. After filtering and drying it results in CP-9 (Sakuramil).

action.title: CPP #4.1 Water addition in the crystallization (% by weight with respect to ethanol)

text.div: PlanDefinition Wet (fluid-bed) granulation, blending, compression and film-coating. Commercial batch size 520.00 kg (approx. 2,600,000 tablets). No overages. Critical steps: granulation (step 3) and compression (step 8); granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness are controlled within a design space to ensure dissolution.

resource.title: Manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablets (Aparna Pharmaceutical Manufacturing)
resource.description: Wet (fluid-bed) granulation, blending, compression and film-coating. Commercial batch size 520.00 kg (approx. 2,600,000 tablets). No overages. Critical steps: granulation (step 3) and compression (step 8); granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness are controlled within a design space to ensure dissolution.

action.title: Step 1 - Pre-blending
action.description: Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance in a diffusion mixer (bin blender).

action.title: Step 2 - Preparation of granulation liquid
action.description: Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

action.title: Step 3 - Granulation
action.description: Load the pre-blended material into a fluid bed granulator and add the granulation liquid to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules.

action.title: Step 4 - Drying
action.description: Dry the granules using the dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit until loss on drying of 1 - 2 % is achieved.

action.title: Step 5 - Screening
action.description: Sieve the dried granules using a screening mill.

action.title: Step 6 - Lubricant addition
action.description: Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen and add it to the granules.

action.title: Step 7 - Final blending
action.description: Blend the mixture using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

action.title: Step 8 - Tablet compression
action.description: Compress the final blend using a tablet press to obtain the tablet cores.

action.title: Step 9 - Preparation of the coating suspension
action.description: Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water.

action.title: Step 10 - Film-coating
action.description: Film-coat the tablet cores using the film-coat suspension in a coating pan to achieve the desired film-coat weight gain, followed by drying.

action.title: Step 11 - Inspection
action.description: Collect 10 tablets to perform the Description test and Identification test (RTRT).

action.title: Step 12 - Primary packaging
action.description: The film-coated tablets are primary packaged (HDPE bottle or PA/AL/PVC blister).

action.title: Step 13 - Secondary packaging
action.description: The primary packaged product is packed in a cardboard-based secondary pack.

resource.description: Wet (fluid-bed) granulation, blending, compression and film-coating. Commercial batch size 520.00 kg (approx. 2,600,000 tablets). No overages. Critical steps: granulation (step 3) and compression (step 8); granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness are controlled within a design space to ensure dissolution.

action.title: Step 1 - Pre-blending
action.description: Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance in a diffusion mixer (bin blender).

action.title: Step 2 - Preparation of granulation liquid
action.description: Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

action.title: Step 3 - Granulation
action.description: Load the pre-blended material into a fluid bed granulator and add the granulation liquid to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules.

action.title: Step 4 - Drying
action.description: Dry the granules using the dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit until loss on drying of 1 - 2 % is achieved.

action.title: Step 5 - Screening
action.description: Sieve the dried granules using a screening mill.

action.title: Step 6 - Lubricant addition
action.description: Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen and add it to the granules.

action.title: Step 7 - Final blending
action.description: Blend the mixture using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

action.title: Step 8 - Tablet compression
action.description: Compress the final blend using a tablet press to obtain the tablet cores.

action.title: Step 9 - Preparation of the coating suspension
action.description: Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water.

action.title: Step 10 - Film-coating
action.description: Film-coat the tablet cores using the film-coat suspension in a coating pan to achieve the desired film-coat weight gain, followed by drying.

action.title: Step 11 - Inspection
action.description: Collect 10 tablets to perform the Description test and Identification test (RTRT).

action.title: Step 12 - Primary packaging
action.description: The film-coated tablets are primary packaged (HDPE bottle or PA/AL/PVC blister).

action.title: Step 13 - Secondary packaging
action.description: The primary packaged product is packed in a cardboard-based secondary pack.

text.div: PlanDefinition Wet (fluid-bed) granulation, blending, compression and film-coating. Commercial batch size 520.00 kg (approx. 2,600,000 tablets). No overages. Critical steps: granulation (step 3) and compression (step 8); granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness are controlled within a design space to ensure dissolution.

resource.title: Manufacturing process of Sakura Bloom 20 mg film-coated tablets (Aparna Pharmaceutical Manufacturing)
resource.description: Wet (fluid-bed) granulation, blending, compression and film-coating. Commercial batch size 520.00 kg (approx. 2,600,000 tablets). No overages. Critical steps: granulation (step 3) and compression (step 8); granule particle size and uncoated tablet hardness are controlled within a design space to ensure dissolution.

action.title: Step 1 - Pre-blending
action.description: Blend 52.000 kg of cellulose, microcrystalline, 26.000 kg of croscarmellose sodium, 353.600 kg of lactose monohydrate and 52.000 kg of Sakuramil drug substance in a diffusion mixer (bin blender).

action.title: Step 2 - Preparation of granulation liquid
action.description: Dissolve 15.600 kg hydroxypropyl cellulose in purified water using a vessel with stirrer to prepare a granulation liquid free from lumps.

action.title: Step 3 - Granulation
action.description: Load the pre-blended material into a fluid bed granulator and add the granulation liquid to achieve wetting of pre-blended material and formation of granules.

action.title: Step 4 - Drying
action.description: Dry the granules using the dryer integrated within the fluid bed granulator unit until loss on drying of 1 - 2 % is achieved.

action.title: Step 5 - Screening
action.description: Sieve the dried granules using a screening mill.

action.title: Step 6 - Lubricant addition
action.description: Sieve 5.200 kg of magnesium stearate through a screen and add it to the granules.

action.title: Step 7 - Final blending
action.description: Blend the mixture using a diffusion mixer (bin blender) to obtain the final blend.

action.title: Step 8 - Tablet compression
action.description: Compress the final blend using a tablet press to obtain the tablet cores.

action.title: Step 9 - Preparation of the coating suspension
action.description: Prepare a homogeneous suspension of the Basic coating premix, red in purified water.

action.title: Step 10 - Film-coating
action.description: Film-coat the tablet cores using the film-coat suspension in a coating pan to achieve the desired film-coat weight gain, followed by drying.

action.title: Step 11 - Inspection
action.description: Collect 10 tablets to perform the Description test and Identification test (RTRT).

action.title: Step 12 - Primary packaging
action.description: The film-coated tablets are primary packaged (HDPE bottle or PA/AL/PVC blister).

action.title: Step 13 - Secondary packaging
action.description: The primary packaged product is packed in a cardboard-based secondary pack.
